**Surat al-Hadid (The Iron)**

Its central purpose is to show the universality of the Messengership in line with the universality of the Divinity, through the sending (to) the three categories mentioned in the two preceding surahs, from both jinn and humankind. This is to confirm that He, glory be to Him, is singled out for all the attributes of perfection, and to confirm His transcendence above every trace of deficiency. This surah begins with the glorification of Allah, and the preceding surah ends with it. It refutes their saying: ﴿Will we indeed be resurrected, or our forefathers of old?﴾ It calls for the striving (jihad) against those who need to be fought against, from among those who disobeyed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), by the sword, along with what follows from that of spending (in the cause of Allah). This is to turn them away from bodily deficiencies and to exalt them toward the spiritual words to which the Book calls, out of fear of an unequal reckoning on the Day of Manifestation, for the separation between the servants with justice. Thus the People of the Book and others will enter the religion willingly or unwillingly, and the People of the Book who used to say, "No one is better than him," will know the excellence of this Messenger (ﷺ) over all the messengers before him, peace be upon them, through the universality of his message, the comprehensiveness of his caliphate, the spread of his call, and the multitude of his community. This is to confirm that there is no limit to the overflowing of His mercy, glory be to Him. Thus this surah, which is the end of the first half, and the one after it, which is the beginning of the second half, in terms of number, serve as the ultimate aim of the purpose of the surah which is its beginning, when considered in relation and response, just as the surah which was the end of the first half in length was (p. 251) al-Isra', and likewise the surah which is the beginning of the second half, al-Kahf, both revealing the aim of the first in what it called to of guidance and what it urged of warning. This is indicated by its name, al-Hadid, through reflecting on its verses and pondering the secret of what is mentioned in it and its aims. The author of al-Firdaws narrates from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not perform cupping (hijamah) on Tuesday, for the surah al-Hadid was revealed on a Tuesday."

(In the name of Allah) whose divinity encompasses all existing things. (The All-Merciful) whose generosity has embraced them in all their movements and rests. (The Most Merciful) who, among them, has singled out by His choice, in perfect power, the people of His guardianship with what pleases Him of acts of worship.

* *

When the discourse of al-Waqi'ah concluded with the command to glorify Him above what the disbelievers denied of resurrection, this surah came to establish that glorification and to clarify it with proof, argument, the sword and the spear. So He, exalted, said, as a rationale for the end of al-Waqi'ah: ﴿Glorifies﴾, that is, let there be glorification by the indication of natural disposition, magnifying Him, glory be to Him, affirming His lordship, and submitting to His obedience. He made the verb intransitive while it is transitive, to indicate generality by its being left unrestricted, and sincerity by its being made to take the preposition "li-" (for). He made it past tense here, and in al-Hashr and al-Saff, and present tense in al-Jumu'ah and al-Taghabun, to indicate that what is attributed to Him of glorification is part of His nature, His constant practice and His habit. Each of the past and present tenses is specified by what it opens with, for what comes at the beginning of al-Jumu'ah. The use of the verbal noun at the beginning of al-Isra' is more eloquent, in that its unrestricted form indicates (p. 252) the deserving of glorification from everything and in every state. ﴿For Allah﴾, that is, the King who encompasses all the attributes of perfection. ﴿Whatever is in the heavens﴾, that is, the lofty bodies and what is in them, and the earth and whoever is in it, and every heaven and whoever is in it, and what is between them, because all of them are within the Throne, which is the highest of creation.

Since the discourse at the end of al-Waqi'ah was addressed to the people of special closeness, indeed to the most special of the people of special closeness, there was no need for emphasis. So He omitted what was made into the two regions (the east and the west) as one thing, because His regard for them is a regard of exaltedness, a single regard, in line with what He reported about them of transcendence. So He said: ﴿And the earth﴾, that is, and what is in it, and likewise the lands themselves, as mentioned before. This includes all existing things, because if all of that glorifies Him, then the glorification of the Throne is by way of priority, and the transcendence of these things by what is in them of signs indicating that He, glory be to Him, is not touched by any trace of deficiency, and that everything stands at the door, witnessing the seeking. Al-Qushayri said: Tasbih (glorification) means sanctification and transcendence, and it may also mean the swimming of secrets in the seas of majesty, so that they attain the jewels of monotheism, string them in the necklace of faith, and adorn them in the collars of union.

When He established this, He indicated that nothing has the power to be separated from Him, and that He has every perfection; so He is the one deserving of glorification and praise. So He said: ﴿And He﴾, that is, He alone, ﴿is the Mighty﴾, who overcomes everything and is not overcome by anything, ﴿the Wise﴾, who perfected everything He made.

And Ustadh Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr al-Asimi said in his Burhan: When His saying, glory be to Him and exalted, ﴿Why then do you not believe?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 57] preceded, and it contains a degree of rebuke and reproach for those who were rebuked by it, which is not hidden, then it was followed by His exalted saying: ﴿Have you considered the semen you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58], the verses up to His saying: ﴿and a provision for the desert travelers﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 73]. They were thus admonished and reproved for the evil of their ignorance and the ugliness of their error. Then He, glory be to Him and exalted, said after that: ﴿Is it this discourse you are scornful of?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 81], and their reproach continued up to His saying: ﴿if you are truthful﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 87]. When these verses pointed to the ugliness of their misdeeds, the Exalted followed that with His transcendence, glory be to Him, above the evil of what they claimed and their error in what they were ignorant of. So He, exalted, said: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 96], that is, transcend Him above their great error and the evil of their audacity. Then He followed that with His saying: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah﴾, that is, glorify by the name of your Lord, for this is the practice of the whole world.

﴿And to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 83]. ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah.﴾ Then He followed that with His saying: ﴿To Him belongs dominion, and to Him belongs praise﴾ [al-Taghabun: 1]. [Thus the Exalted made clear His being singled out with the attribute of majesty and the descriptions of perfection, and that He is the one alone with dominion and praise,] and that He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, up to His saying: ﴿and He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [al-Hadid: 6]. These verses thus included the humbling of those whose condition was alluded to in the preceding verse of surah al-Waqi'ah, and the cutting off of their error, and the informing them of what they were ignorant of regarding His exalted attributes and His beautiful names, exalted is He. The verses of the two surahs began and their meanings were connected. Then He turned the address to His believing servants, so He, exalted, said: ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hadid: 7], and the verses continued addressing them until the end of the surah. End of quotation.

(p-254) When He had informed of that, He indicated, in an explicit manner, what the first [clause] had implied concerning the glorification of the heavens and the earth, by saying: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, to Him alone; i.e., the dominion of what is in them and between them, outwardly and inwardly. The outward dominion is what now exists in this world: an earth spread out, a heaven constructed, luminous stars, lofty spheres, perceptible winds, and visible clouds, along with whatever is detailed beyond these of creation and command. The inward dominion is that which is hidden from us, and the greatest of it is what is attributed to the Other, namely the malakut (the invisible realm of sovereignty). Al-Qushayri said: "Al-mulk (dominion) is an intensive form of al-milk (ownership), by the indication of the damma (the u-vowel). He said: al-milk with a kasra means the power to originate, so there is no owner except God. When it is said of other than Him that he is "malik" (an owner), it is in a metaphorical sense, through the rulings connected in the Law to people's ownership, that is, by validating it or invalidating it and the like." Thus the verse is of the type of ihtibak (complementary omission): it mentioned what is between the heavens and the earth first, as evidence for the omission of what is between them the second time, and it mentioned the two horizons (east and west) second, as evidence for the omission of the like of that the first time, so that the glorification and the dominion encompass all.

Since that is something not in dispute, and since a contrarian might perhaps dispute it, He indicated it by means of something no one else could hope for, and so He said, placing the giving of life first because it is so in external reality, and because the period of life is greater, since resurrection is an everlasting life after which there is no death: ﴿He gives life﴾, that is, He possesses the attribute of giving life, so He gives life to whom He wills of creation, by bringing it into being with the attribute of life in whatever way He wills, in stages which He turns through as He wills, and as He wills and of whom He wills (p-255) ﴿and causes to die﴾, that is, He possesses these two attributes by way of choice, renewal and continuance. Thus He is able to resurrect, by the evidence of the attribute of giving life established for Him. Since this encompasses the power of renewal and of return, He generalized the ruling by saying: ﴿and He is over all things﴾, that is, of giving life, causing death and other things, of every possible thing, ﴿Competent﴾, that is, reaching the utmost degree of power beyond which no increase is possible.

When He had informed of the completeness of power, He indicated this by His saying: ﴿He﴾, that is, He alone, ﴿is the First﴾, that is, by pre-eternity (al-azaliyya), before everything, so He has no beginning. He is the Eternal (al-qadim) from whom the existence of everything comes, and His existence is not from anything, because everything we observe is subject to change, since it is contingent (haqir), and whatever is like that must have an originator that is not subject to change. ﴿And the Last﴾ by everlastingness (al-abadiyya), in whom the existence of everything ends in the chain of ascent, and who is after the annihilation of everything, even if considered in terms of what belongs to Him from His own essence. He has no end, because the attribute of non-existence (al-'adam) is impossible for Him, since everything other than Him is changeable, and whatever changes in any kind of change is possibly annihilated, and whatever is possibly annihilated must have an annihilator that comes after it, and it is not possible for Him to be annihilated.

Since precedence (al-sabq) requires being hidden (al-buṭūn), and lateness (al-ta'akhkhur) requires being manifest (al-ẓuhūr), and these are two opposing matters that a human being can hardly attach to one thing at once, He drew attention to their combination in Him, and said, indicating with the conjunction "wa" (and) the completeness of the attribute and its realization: ﴿And the Manifest﴾, that is, by oneness (al-aḥadiyya) to the intellect through its manifest proofs in created things, through what belongs to Him of acts, a manifestness that no sensible person ignores, and He is the dominant one in His exaltedness and loftiness, so there is nothing above Him. (p-256) ﴿And the Hidden﴾ by self-sufficient eternity (al-ṣamadiyya), and by being beyond the imprinting of the senses, the stamping of the imagination, and the conception of understanding and thought, and by the completeness of knowledge and wisdom, with what belongs to Him of greatness in His essence, through the multitude of His transcendence and veils, a hiddenness that nothing encompasses. Al-Qushayri said: "The First without beginning, the Last without end, the Manifest without concealment, the Hidden in the attribute of exaltedness and the might of greatness." End of quotation. The conjunction serves to indicate, as has been pointed out, the complete encompassing. Because these attributes are opposites, if they were stripped of the "wa", one might think that their existence is not in the manner of full establishment, and so they would not be encompassing but restricted by some aspect, for example. Therefore the "wa" came to indicate the establishment of the attribute and its comprehensiveness, and that it applies in every respect; none of the attributes is completing something else or explaining its meaning. So He is the First absolutely and the Last likewise, and Manifest even in the state of His being hidden, and Hidden likewise. This is according to the original principle, for His attributes, exalted is He, encompass one another, so there is no difficulty. The difficulty arises only when the conjunction is absent, and that is the more common form in their citation, as in ﴿the First and the Last﴾ ... and perhaps this is the meaning of al-Kashshaf's statement: the first "wa" means it indicates the combining of the two attributes of firstness and lastness, a combining that is in the utmost possibility; the third indicates that He is the combiner of manifestness and hiddenness; and as for the middle one, it indicates that He is the combiner of the whole of the first two attributes and the whole of the last two, so He is the one whose existence is continuous at all past and future times. End of quotation.

Since whoever is manifest to one thing is hidden from another, and whoever is hidden from one thing is absent from its knowledge, and since He, glorified is He, is in His manifestness in the sense that nothing is above Him, and in His hiddenness in the sense that nothing is beneath Him, the attributes have combined the encompassing of knowledge and power. He then informed of the result of that, saying: ﴿And He is Knower of all things﴾, that is, because all things are equal in relation to Him. The hiddenness and manifestness are only relative to the creation; as for Him, glorified is He, there is no hidden thing of the creation before Him, but rather He is in utmost manifestness before Him, because He is the One who brought them into existence. This is the meaning of what al-Baghawi, may God have mercy on him, said: "'Umar, may God be pleased with him, asked Ka'b about this verse, and he said: its meaning is that His knowledge of the First is like His knowledge of the Last, and His knowledge of the Manifest is like His knowledge of the Hidden." End of quotation.

Because knowledge necessarily entails power according to its measure.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 57, verse 4:

Since the maker of a thing must know it, the text has indicated His knowledge, and what preceded of His attributes, by His saying: ﴿He﴾, that is, He alone, ﴿who created the heavens﴾, and He used the plural for them because of the Arabs' knowledge of their multiplicity, ﴿and the earth﴾, that is, the genus that encompasses all of them. He used the singular for it because they had not reached knowledge of its multiplicity, ﴿in six days﴾, as a way of establishing deliberateness (*ta'annin*) and confirming the days, which He made odd by making the seventh the day in which He created man. The name of that day, *al-Jumu'ah* (Friday), indicates that man is the ultimate intended purpose and that the day is the seventh, which shows that he is the end of the created things. This is the end of the quotation.

Since the king's taking his seat on the throne of kingship is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for his sole management and the encompassing of his power and knowledge, and since this is the essence of kingship, the text indicated it, drawing attention to His greatness by using the particle of delay (*thumma*), and said: ﴿then He established Himself﴾, that is, He brought into being *al-sawa'*, which is justice, in the manner of one who is intensely concerned, ﴿upon the Throne﴾, which encompasses all existing things, through a firm management of the Throne and what is beneath it and beneath whom, so that the servants may conceive that the Throne is the source of management and the locus of decree, as we say of our kings: "So-and-so sat upon the throne of kingship," meaning that he alone manages affairs, even though there may be no throne at all, let alone sitting.

Since the intended meaning of *istiwa'* is sole management, and management cannot be valid except through knowledge and power, He clarified it by His saying, indicating that His knowledge of hidden things is like His knowledge of manifest things: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾, that is, what enters in a way that causes it to disappear, ﴿and what emerges from it﴾, that is, of plants and other things, and parts of the dead and others. [And although] this is far from the Throne, all places are equal with respect to Him in nearness and distance. ﴿And what comes out of it﴾, likewise. The use of the present tense indicates the powers He has deposited in the two regions, so that by His creation these things are renewed from them continuously, a continuity that lasts until their ruin.

Since He established this regarding what may be thought to be distant because of its lowness and distance from the Throne, as a warning against being confined to a place, and since it was more appropriate to mention it first, He followed it with its counterpart, which is the direction of height, to generalize His action over all creation. He said: ﴿and what descends from the sky﴾, and He did not use the plural, (p. 259) because the intended meaning is achieved by the singular, and expressing it in the singular conveys the lowest genus of all of them. This includes revelation, rains, heat, cold, and other existing things and benefits which He, glorified is He, brings into being, such as the measures of the lifespans of the children of Adam, their provisions, and all other aspects of their affairs. ﴿And what ascends into it﴾, that is, rises, climbs, and disappears into it, ﴿such as vapors, lights, stars, deeds, and others.﴾

Since one whose dominion is vast may lose knowledge of some part of it because of its distance from him, the text made clear that there is no distance at all between Him and any of the things, and so He said: ﴿And He is with you﴾, that is, O you two weights (*al-thaqalan*, jinn and humankind), who need refinement through knowledge and power, which are caused by nearness, ﴿wherever you may be﴾. So He knows all your affairs and has power over you, exalted above any conjunction with knowledge and contact, or separation from it through absence or distance. Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyya said in his book *al-Furqan Bayn Awliya' al-Rahman wa-Awliya' al-Shaytan*: The word "ma'a" (with) in the language of the Arabs does not require that one of the two things be mixed with the other, as in His saying: ﴿Fear God and be with the truthful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 119], and His saying: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. The word "ma'a" occurs in the Qur'an in both a general and a specific sense. The general sense is in His saying: ﴿There is no secret conference of three but that He is their fourth, nor of five but that He is their sixth, nor fewer than that nor more, but He is with them﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7], to the end of the verse. He opened the statement with knowledge and closed it with knowledge. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, al-Dahhak, (p. 260) Sufyan al-Thawri, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: "He is with them by His knowledge." As for the specific sense of being with, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾ [al-Nahl: 128], and His saying to Musa and Harun, peace be upon them: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46], and He said: ﴿When he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed God is with us"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40], meaning the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him. So He is with Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, and not with Pharaoh; and with Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companion, may God be pleased with him, and not with Abu Jahl or others of his enemies; and with those who fear Him and those who do good, and not with the wrongdoers and transgressors. If the meaning of being with were that He is in His essence in every place, the specific and general statements would contradict one another. Rather, the meaning is that He is with these by His help and support and not with those. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the one who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 84], that is, He is God in the heaven and God on the earth, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs the highest description in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Rum: 27]. Likewise in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is God in the heavens and in the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 3], as the leading scholars of knowledge such as Ahmad and others explained it, that He is the one worshipped in the heavens and the earth.

Since deeds have an outward and an inward aspect, He expressed their matter by the name of the Essence (*Allah*), indicating that they are comprehensively encompassed by His knowledge and power, and drawing attention to the greatness of the encompassing of them and of every one of His attributes. He said: ﴿And God﴾, that is, the one who encompasses all the attributes of perfection. He placed the prepositional phrase first to give added emphasis and to draw attention to the certainty of encompassing, as the point was already noted (p. 261) several times, and its illustration by such phrases as: "I know so-and-so and I know no one else." He said: ﴿sees what you do﴾, that is, in a manner of continuous renewal and persistence, ﴿All-Seeing﴾, that is, knowing its grand and subtle details.

Since the maker of a thing may not be its king, and a king's kingship is not complete unless he knows everything that happens in his kingdom and has power over it, and since their denial of resurrection amounted to a denial that He is King, He confirmed this by repeating the report about it, saying: ﴿To Him alone belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾ — He said "heavens" in the plural because the context calls for it — ﴿and the earth﴾ — He said "earth" in the singular because its multiplicity was hidden from them, while the generic sense is intended. He indicated the lasting nature of His dominion and its all-encompassing scope by His words, coordinating with what is implied as its meaning: ﴿So from Allah is the beginning﴾, expressing Himself with the supreme, all-comprehensive Name, lest it be thought that the statement is restricted to the matters mentioned earlier: ﴿And to Allah﴾ — that is, to the King who has no equal, alone — ﴿all matters are returned﴾ — in every respect, with the utmost ease — that is, all of them, sensibly through resurrection and in meaning through origination and cessation. He indicated this origination and cessation with the most wondrous and splendid of affairs, and so He said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 6:

﴿Yūlij﴾ means: He causes to enter and makes disappear, through diminution and effacement, ﴿the night into the day﴾. So the night, after its length, becomes short, and after its being a manifest presence and its descent, it is erased, and then light fills the horizons after that darkness. ﴿And He causes the day to enter﴾ which its light has encompassed the whole of existence, and whose radiance has illuminated it, ﴿into the night﴾ which had been hidden in His knowledge, so that darkness has covered the horizons, and the length which it had has become a deficiency.

Since this contains the manifestation of the most hidden of things until it becomes in the utmost clarity, He follows it with knowledge of what is most hidden to people, and says: ﴿And He﴾ that is, alone ﴿is All-Knowing﴾ that is, of perfect knowledge ﴿of what is within the breasts﴾ that is, what accompanies them, so that they conceal it, and so the stirrings of thoughts do not emerge from them over the course of days, despite their great variety, change and alteration, even though they are hidden from their own possessors.

When the proofs had established His transcendence, glorified be He, above any trace of imperfection, and His encompassing of every attribute of perfection, which necessitates that dominion belongs to Him, and which necessarily entails that He alone is God in the fullest sense, and which requires sending a messenger to all who are in His dominion whom He wills, and He concluded with knowledge of the inner thoughts, the most excellent of which is faith, He said, commanding submission to Him and to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿Believe﴾, i.e., O you two weighty groups (humans and jinn), ﴿in God﴾, i.e., the Greatest King who has no like, ﴿and His Messenger﴾, whose greatness derives from His greatness. And since faith is the foundation, and spending is the visible face and the head, He combined the hidden supporting foundation with the complete, radiant, visible face, saying: ﴿And spend﴾, i.e., in making His religion manifest. He encouraged them to do so by asking for what is little of what He has given them [God], and made them detached from it by His saying: ﴿of that which He has made you﴾, i.e., by His power, ﴿successors in﴾, i.e., your succession to it being something sought and existing, ﴿it﴾, and it belongs to Him, not to you, through what pleases the One who appointed you as successors in paving His way. So be content in your souls to give it, for in reality it is not yours; you are only custodians. And fear being removed from succession by its being snatched from your hands and entrusted to others, either during your lives, or (p-263) after your deaths, as He did with others when He brought to you what reached you of their wealth. So there is nothing for you of it except what you eat and thereby consume, or what you wear and thereby wear out, or what you give in charity and thereby preserve. And in another narration: "what you have enacted." Let spending from it be easy for you, just as it is easy for a person to spend from the wealth of another when that person has permitted him to do so.

When He commanded spending and described it with what makes it easy, He made the promise of what encourages it a consequence of this, stressing the promise emphatically, because of the hardship involved in doing it, by expressing it with a nominal sentence, by basing the judgment on the pronoun, by describing it with greatness, and in other ways. He said: ﴿So those who believe﴾ among you, and He made clear that this is specific to them because of the straitened circumstances of their time, saying: ﴿from among you and spend﴾, i.e., from their wealth in the ways to which He urged them, in the manner of setting things right, as the expression "spend" indicates. ﴿For them is a great reward﴾, i.e., your minds cannot reach the reality of its greatness. So seize the opportunity to spend during your days of succession, before your removal from it and your loss of it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 57, verse 8:

When he (Allah) had encouraged them to spend and to believe, and belief necessarily entails spending, He marvelled at those who do not hasten to attain every good. So He said, detailing what had been stated in general terms of the encouragement to both, beginning with the clearest of all good, easing their hearts by using the particle of the future (*lā* with the imperfect) in announcing forgiveness of the past. He warned and rebuked those who do not hasten to what the interrogative particle governs, and the construction is coordinated with an implied clause, meaning: "Then what is wrong with you that you do not hasten to that?" ﴿And what﴾, i.e., and what reason or excuse, or anything else, ﴿is [there] for you﴾ that ﴿you do not believe in Allah﴾, i.e., you do not renew belief, meaning renewal that is continuous, ﴿in the Sovereign, the Most High﴾, i.e., the One to whom belongs all sovereignty and all command, ﴿after you hear this message?﴾ Because *lā* (not) does not precede an imperfect verb except when it carries the meaning of the future. Had he expressed it with a form indicating the present, some stubborn disputant might have said, "Bring what is demanded of us." What follows this, in the form of a circumstantial clause that has the sense of a cause, indicates this, and it is His saying: ﴿while the Messenger﴾, i.e., while the one who holds the general message, ﴿calls you﴾ morning and evening, in view of what is required for acceptance of him, such as his good bearing, the greatness of his station, the manifestation of extraordinary signs, and other things, ﴿that you may believe﴾, i.e., in order that you renew belief ﴿in your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who nurtured you well by making you of the community of this noble Prophet ﷺ and honouring you with him. ﴿And He has already taken your covenant﴾, i.e., the covenant has indeed been taken, so that abandoning that by which trust was established becomes supremely ugly, through the setting up of proofs and the enabling of reflection through the creation of minds. All of this is joined to the taking of the offspring from the loins of Adam, peace be upon him, and making them witness against themselves, and the witnessing of the angels over them. In the recitation of Abu 'Amr the verb is put in the passive form (*ukhidha*), so that the meaning is "whatever taking it was," because betrayal is severe among the noble, without regard to any specific party, especially among the Arabs. How much more so when the one who takes is the Greatest King, Capable of everything, All-Knowing of everything, and His Messenger, whose honour is part of honouring Him. This is made clear by the recitation of the majority, which uses the active form (*akhadha*). The grammatical analysis (*i'rāb*) is not obscure. The summary is that they broke the covenant in belief, so He did not seize them until He sent the Messengers.

When He urged them to renew belief continuously, by expressing wonder at their neglect of that, and since each one claimed nobility in goodness, He stirred them and inflamed them with His saying: ﴿if you are﴾, i.e., by innate nature and as an established attribute, ﴿believers﴾, i.e., rooted and firm in the quality of faith, which is to remain upon the light of the original natural disposition (*fiṭra*).

When He described Him with lordship (rububiyyah), He pointed to it by His saying: ﴿He it is﴾, that is, He alone [not other than Him], ﴿who sends down﴾, that is, by way of gradualness (tadarruj) and succession (muwalah), according to need. Since the address in this surah is to the sincere (al-mukhlas), He said, attributing the pronoun to Himself without anything that indicates majesty and grandeur: ﴿to His servant﴾, that is, the one who is most deserving of the presence of His beauty and honour, because he never worshipped anyone other than Him. ﴿Signs﴾, that is, indications which, by their manifestation, are truly such that one should refer to them and be bound by them, ﴿clear﴾ [Fatir: 40] exceedingly so, with the attributes they possess that are in the utmost clarity. ﴿That He may bring you out﴾, that is, Allah, that is, His servant, by what He has been sent down to him, although he is a human being like you; and the kind inclines toward its own kind and is more receptive to it, especially if he is near and wise and discerning. ﴿From the darknesses﴾ in which you are immersed, arising from the appetites and deficiencies with which man was created, and from heedlessness and forgetfulness, which lead to the accumulation of ignorance. Whoever is given knowledge and faith by Him, glorified is He, has indeed brought him out of these darknesses that have come upon him, ﴿into the light﴾, which was the attribute of his spirit and his original, sound nature.

Since the implicit sense is: "Indeed Allah is, with you, Gentle and All-Aware," He followed it with His saying, emphasising it to address the disquiet of those among the believers who are long afflicted by trial, and the denial of the disbelievers: ﴿And indeed Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿toward you﴾. He placed the prepositional phrase first, because the great mercy He has shown to this community necessitates that His favour upon others, in comparison with His favour upon us, be counted as nothing. ﴿Is surely Kind and Merciful﴾. That is, you are, in view of His special mercy, which is for the completion of favour, of two categories: among you is one who had a connection with Him through what he did in the days of ignorance of good deeds such as spending in the way of what is right, and he expressed it with "spending" because it is good, without show or the like in it, like al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, so that after the general mercy of clarification, a great mercy returned to him, specifically, which brought him to the highest degrees of gnosis (irfan). And among you is one who was extreme in following his desire, so after the general mercy of clarification, He began with him a special mercy by which He guided him to the works of the Gardens, and it is less than what came before it in the balance. And above it in that it is without any cause on the part of the one shown mercy.

(p. 267) When He commanded them to believe and to spend, and faith, though it is the foundation without which no deed is valid, is free of any loss or deficiency, He began with it for that reason. He encouraged [the believer] by ending the verse with the mention of compassion (*ra'fah*), indicating that [whoever] reaches Him with some faith or other [act] is increased by Him from His bounty. [This is in line with] "Whoever draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit... up to his saying: and whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running" (*harwalah*). Then He connected to it the exhortation to reach Him through spending. He rebuked those who abandon it and reproached those who turn away from it while knowing that it is perishable, and by the addition of *'an* (the verbal *'an*) he conveyed blame for leaving it in all three tenses. So He said: ﴿And what⦆ meaning, and what thing comes about ﴿for you﴾ in ﴿not spending﴾, meaning, bringing into existence the expenditure of wealth ﴿in the way of God﴾, meaning in everything that pleases the Greatest King, who possesses the attributes of perfection, so that you may have a connection to Him, and He will single you out with compassion, which is the greatest of mercy. For no one withholds [it] from a good cause except that God empowers over him a loss in an evil cause. He placed the explicit noun in the place of the pronoun within a circumstantial clause, prompting spending with the most eloquent urging, and so He said: ﴿And to God﴾, affirming His greatness by urging that [spending] by recalling all the attributes of perfection, especially the attribute of inheritance, which requires detachment from what is inherited ﴿is the inheritance﴾ [i.e.] the act of inheriting, the thing inherited, the one from whom it is inherited, and other than that ﴿of the heavens and the earth﴾, all together, with nothing in them or from them [belonging to anyone] except Him. Thus it departs from whoever benefits from it, and remains for God as the inheritance remains. Whoever reflects that he himself is perishing, and all that is in his hand, and that death is behind him, and that the grip of the calamities of events is closing upon him, and that what is in his hand will soon be transferred to another, will find generosity with his self and wealth easy.

When He encouraged them to spend in general, He encouraged them to hasten to it, praising its people, singling out from among them the people of foremost rivalry. So He said: ﴿Not equal﴾. Since the intended meaning is the people of Islam, He clarified by His saying: ﴿among you are those who spent﴾, meaning, brought into existence spending from their wealth, all their strength, and whatever they are able to do. Since the intended meaning is spending during the time of faith and not any time at all, He restricted it with the prepositional phrase and said: ﴿before the conquest﴾, meaning the conquest which is in reality the conquest of the whole world, namely the conquest of Mecca, which was the cause of the religion's manifestation over all [other] religion, because of what the spender then encountered through spending: great hardships due to the narrowness of wealth at that time. That entails that the spender had a more penetrating insight, his expenditure was greater in sufficiency, and more beneficial. In this is evidence of the excellence of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, for he was the first to spend, and no one preceded him in that. In regard to it the verse was revealed, as al-Baghawi related from al-Kalbi.

Since the intended meaning of faith is service to the All-Merciful, and spending, although it confirms faith, is not perfected in its affirmation except by giving up the self, He said: ﴿and fought﴾, meaning striving in spending his self for the sake of the one in whom he believed. He omitted the negated part for the sake of equating it with [the one who] did not spend at all, or [did not spend] with the restriction of priority, because of what follows it. Perhaps He used the singular pronoun to indicate the fewness of the foremost.

Since negating equality does not by itself distinguish the excellent from others, and the counterpart of "those who spent" was omitted for its clarity, for its repulsiveness, and because what follows indicates it, He removed the ambiguity with His saying: ﴿Those﴾, meaning the spenders who fought, who are the foremost, the first among the emigrants and the helpers, nearest to the people of the lofty rank because of their hastening to generosity with self and wealth. ﴿are greater in rank﴾, and with the greatness of rank comes the greatness of its possessor ﴿than those who spent﴾. Since the intended meaning is the preference over those who brought spending and fighting into existence [in a time after that, not over those who occupied every time after it with spending and fighting], He introduced the prepositional phrase and said: ﴿after [that] and fought﴾. Since preference implies that all share in the excellence, He stated it explicitly, encouraging spending in every circumstance, and so He said: ﴿And to each﴾, meaning of the two categories, ﴿God has promised﴾ [i.e.] He who possesses majesty, perfection, and honor ﴿the best﴾, meaning the rank which is the ultimate of goodness, even though it varies in itself. Ibn 'Amir read ﴿And each﴾, and it is more in harmony with what it is joined to.

Since the purification of deeds is only by intentions, and preference is the criterion of knowledge, He said, encouraging good intentions and warning against falling short in them: ﴿And God﴾, meaning He who has all-encompassing comprehension of every attribute of perfection. He placed the prepositional phrase first to indicate greater care in distinguishing at the time of preference, and so He said: ﴿is Aware of what you do﴾, meaning you renew its doing over the passage of times, ﴿All-Aware﴾, meaning, knowing its inward and outward [aspects] with a knowledge that admits no increase in any respect (p. 270). He therefore makes the reward of deeds proportionate to the measure of the intentions, which are the spirits of their forms.

When He had given preference to those who spent before the conquest, and had promised the best reward to those who followed later with good adherence, and indicated that He might join the latter to some of the former through the purity of sincerity, so that the motives to giving became abundant, this led to His saying, naming the charity whose outward form is giving without return by the name of a loan, which is giving with return, in order to encourage people to it because of the certain reward He has prepared for it, so how much more so when it is multiplied: ﴿Who﴾, and He emphasized it with the demonstrative in His saying ﴿this﴾, because of the stinginess that is in souls. ﴿Is it he who lends to God﴾, meaning, gives to the One who possesses all the attributes of majesty and generosity, by giving to the deserving one for His sake a gift from his wealth, in the form of a loan, hoping for the reward. ﴿A goodly loan﴾, meaning, a good, pure loan, sincere in it, seeking in it the best of ways, with the soul willing to give it, without reminders, without distress, and without delay or the like.

Since what God gives the one who spends in return is a consequence of his spending, He linked it with the particle *fa* (then), saying, in coordination with ﴿lends﴾: ﴿then He will multiply it for him﴾, encouraging it by making the multiplication intensive at first (*fa-yuḍā'ifahu* with the form of intensification), and by making it of the *mufā'alah* form (the third verbal pattern, denoting reciprocal or repeated action) secondly. Likewise the emphasis (is in the reading of Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub) *fa-yuḍ'ifahu*, and Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it in the accusative case as an answer to the interrogative, to emphasize the connection and causation. Since the multiplication from Him, glorified is He, is something whose reality none knows except Him, He said: ﴿And for him﴾, that is, for the lender, beyond what you comprehend of the multiplication, an increase upon that: ﴿a generous reward﴾, whose measure none knows except God. This is the meaning of His describing it by saying ﴿noble﴾, that is, good, pure, growing and abundant.

[p. 271]

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 12:

When he had explained what is due to this lender, he described part of his generosity by specifying its time, saying: ﴿On the Day﴾, that is, for them this will be at the time when ﴿you see﴾ [with the eye] ﴿the believing men and the believing women﴾ — indicating that what is beloved of wealth is not parted with, especially in times of hardship, except by one whose religion has taken root in his heart, which is expressed by describing them with the attribute: ﴿the believing men and the believing women﴾, that is, those for whom faith has become a firmly established quality. ﴿Their light runs﴾ before them and on their right hands as a sign of their felicity, ﴿their light﴾, which makes them see everything that benefits them so they take it, and everything that harms them so they abandon it. This is in proportion to their righteous deeds which they used to perform by the light of knowledge, which is the fruit of faith, just as they had put forward wealth, which a person acquires only for such a purpose, as a fitting recompense.

Since whoever is to be honored is given what is due and what follows it in noble places that he loves, He said: ﴿Before them﴾, that is, wherever they turn, and for this reason (p-272) he omitted the preposition ﴿and on their right﴾ [that is], and it adheres to that direction, because these two directions are the noblest of their directions. They are either among the foremost, or among the People of the Right, and they are given their records from these two directions. The wretched one is the opposite of that: he has no light, and his record is given to him in his left hand and from behind his back. The first is the light of faith, knowledge and righteous deeds; the second is the light of spending, because it is with faith — [it was] — pointed out by al-Razi.

When he mentioned their authority in what they love of directions and its facilitation for them, he followed it with what is said to them of what is beloved in their conduct toward that beloved, saying: ﴿Good news for you today﴾, that is, your great glad tidings in everything that awaits you of time.

When they longed for that, they were informed of what is announced, by his saying, informing, indicating that what is informed of is envied among glad tidings because it is the source of joy: ﴿Gardens﴾, that is, existing for you, in which you exercise the greatest disposal. The report in its original sense is entry, but he turned from it to what was mentioned of exaggeration. Then he described them with what delight is not complete without: He said: ﴿flowing﴾, and he conveyed nearness by affirming the preposition, saying: ﴿beneath them rivers﴾. And since that is not complete with fear of cessation, he said: ﴿abiding therein﴾, an abiding without any end, because Allah has bequeathed you that which is not inherited from you, as the rulers of the world do, because in Paradise there is no death. And since this is a delightful matter in that straitened station, loved by a matter, he resumed praising it by his saying: ﴿That﴾, that is, this very great matter, ﴿it is﴾, that is, alone, (p-273) ﴿the great triumph﴾, that is, which by its greatness has filled all directions of your essences, your bodies, your souls and your spirits.

When He had magnified this noble reward by describing what belongs to its people at the time in which it occurs, He magnified it further by describing the torment of their opposites. He said, substituting for the first time expression: ﴿On the day when the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women will say﴾, meaning a renewed statement, given the great and arduous matters that compel it, ﴿to those who believed﴾, meaning in appearance and in reality. As for those among the believers who are above this rank, and those above them, the apparent meaning is that they do not see them, so that they might hope to call out to them. "How far is the Pleiades from the hand of one who reaches for it." ﴿Wait for us﴾, meaning: wait for us by remaining in your places so that we may catch up with you. The verb appears to have been used without its object in the reading of the majority (qira'at al-jama'a, the common reading) because the situation calls for brevity, to the extent that the capacity of the one requesting can reach, out of fear of missing out, since those being addressed hasten to Paradise like a flashing lightning. The reading of Hamza, with the hamza elided and the zay vowelled with a kasra (qira'at Hamza, a canonical recitation), has realised the meaning: that is, make us go slower in walking, be patient with us, and allow us time, do not ask us to hasten in it, but remain in your places so that we may consider how we might catch up with you. The sum is that they regarded their patience in walking and their lingering so that they might catch up with them as a granting of respite to them. ﴿Let us borrow from your light﴾, meaning: let us take, kindle, and seek illumination from it, ﴿from your light﴾, meaning this which we see for you, and none of it reaches us, just as in the world we saw your faith through what we saw of your outward appearances, and we did not gain anything from that as a fitting recompense. The cause of this statement is that they will be given light along with the believers as a deception for them, in return for their deceiving in the world, so that the hardship of losing it will be intensified for them, because soon God will send upon them a wind and darkness that will extinguish their light, and they will remain in the darkness. To this refers the saying of the believers: ﴿Perfect for us our light﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8], meaning: do not extinguish it as You extinguished the light of the hypocrites.

Since what causes them distress is only the rebuff, from whichever speaker it comes, he put the verb in the passive form when saying: ﴿It will be said﴾, meaning to them, as an answer to their request, a statement of rejection, reproach, mockery, and censure: ﴿Return behind you﴾, meaning in all the directions behind you, which are the most distant directions from good, just as in the world you kept turning back on your heels from what deserves to be turned towards and pursued. ﴿Then seek﴾, by reason of that return, ﴿light﴾. It is also possible that "behind" is meant as the world, because this light comes only from it, by reason of the pure deeds and clear knowledge which they practised in it. For this reason, Imam al-Ghazali, may God Most High have mercy on him, said in the Book of Love in the Ihya' (Revival of the Religious Sciences): this verse indicates that lights must have their origin renewed in this world and then increase in brightness in the Hereafter; as for their being renewed there with no light here, that is not so.

Since the implied sense is: so they returned, or so they remained in the darkness, he attached to it and made follow it his statement: ﴿So a wall was struck﴾, in the passive form in the same manner as the first, and to convey that the striking happened with the greatest speed and ease. It is also permissible that the fa' (then) is connected to what precedes it without any implied omission. ﴿Between them﴾, meaning across [the whole of] the distance that lies between those who believed and their opposites at the time of this statement of theirs.

Since the aim is that its striking occurred with the greatest speed, he did not attach the verb to a subject, and he used the fa' so as to convey that it was as if a rod had been struck against the earth in a single blow. So he said: ﴿with a wall﴾, meaning an encompassing barrier, dividing between Paradise and Hellfire, from which none of them escapes and from which none of those other than them can pass over to them. ﴿Having a gate﴾, guarded by a veil, which they open only for those among the believers whom God permits, by what their light, which is before them, guides them to, for intercession or something similar. ﴿Its inner side﴾, meaning the wall and the gate, which is on the side of those who believed, as a recompense for their faith, which is unseen. ﴿Within it is mercy﴾, which is the honour they have in Paradise, which covers the inner part of those in it with its trees and its causes, just as their inner selves were filled with mercy. ﴿And its outer side﴾, meaning of the wall or the gate, which appears to the people of the Fire, begins ﴿from before it﴾, meaning opposite that outer side, on its side, its direction, and with it, ﴿is the torment﴾ of the Fire and its preliminaries, because its people are restricted to outward appearances without having any access to the inner part, the reverse of what they intended by guarding their outward appearances in the world while their inner selves were corrupt. And it indicates what the use of the present tense in "says" implied of repetition, with his statement, as a resumption (isti'naf, a new sentence that begins a fresh thought):

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 14:**

﴿They will call out to them﴾, meaning the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women, will keep calling out to the believers while they are in the darkness, speaking gently to them for the duration of this speech and this blow: ﴿Were we not with you?﴾, meaning in our entirety (p-276) ﴿with you﴾, meaning in the religion you were in, so that we would deserve to share in what you have come to because of that [religion] which we were with you in. ﴿They will say﴾, meaning the believers: ﴿Yes﴾, you were indeed with us, ﴿but you led yourselves into temptation﴾, meaning you were, through the wavering you had, testing ﴿yourselves﴾, mixing with them through testing the states of the religion in a way that transformed them and turned them away from what they were upon of the original nature of uprightness. You wanted by this that apparent, sensory matters would appear to you in it, so that you would be freed in it from doubts and become sincere. But you did not believe in the unseen, so you destroyed yourselves, and you also followed the matters with which you were tempted [by] the desires, and so you made for yourselves the turning away from the lofty inner realities. ﴿And you waited﴾, meaning you burdened yourselves, having removed them from the original nature, so you delayed and waited so that you might see the matter with your own eyes, or you did not act as we did in believing in the unseen, abandoning testing, and attributing what befalls us, which contains trial, to our own selves through our shortcoming. Whenever something befell us that shook us, we would say: "This is what God and His Messenger promised, and God and His Messenger spoke truly," and that only increased us in faith and submission. You also waited for the reversals of fortune to befall the people of faith so that you might display hypocrisy. ﴿And you doubted﴾, meaning you cast doubt, by burdening yourselves with doubt through that waiting. ﴿And false hopes deluded you﴾, meaning what you wish for and estimate of the desires accompanied by great appetite, from empty longings that have no cause other than the soul's craving for them, through what you anticipated for us of misfortunes. ﴿Until the command of God came﴾, meaning the decree of the King who is characterized by all attributes of perfection, so there is no equal to Him and no reversal of His word, [namely] death, and the preliminaries of astonishing matters. (p-277) Just as you were negligent in this world, so you were in this station. ﴿And the Deceiver deluded you concerning God﴾, meaning concerning the King who possesses all greatness, so He is such that He does not break His promise, and He is the Loving Friend. ﴿The Deceiver﴾, meaning the one whose only craft is falsehood, and he is Satan, the enemy and envier. He, through his deception, varies for you the procrastination and says: Indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful, [and] Pardoning and Generous, and what could your sins be in His sight when He is Great, Benevolent, and Forbearing, and the like of this. He does not cease until he brings a person down, and when he has brought him down, he continues upon him with the like of this until he persists, and when he persists, the one who motivates him at that point comes from his own self, and he becomes subject to his hand.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 15:

When they had acknowledged to them the comprehensive state (al-kawn al-jami') and mentioned what had brought it about and the preventing separation, it became clear that there was no such state. They connected to this their saying: ﴿So today no ransom shall be taken﴾, that is, because of those deeds of yours, ﴿from you﴾ (yu'khadhu) is in the passive voice, because the harm lies in the absence of taking, not in its being taken from a specific taker, and in order to convey the closing of the door of taking altogether; ﴿nor from those who disbelieved﴾ ransom (fidyah), that is, a kind of ransom, namely an exchange or a ransom-payment for the self, in any condition, whether small or great, good or otherwise, because God is Self-Sufficient and the place of action that He legislated for the saving of your souls has already passed.

When they were deniers, He emphasized, saying: ﴿nor from those who disbelieved﴾, that is, those who openly displayed their disbelief and did not conceal it as you concealed it, because you are equal to them in disbelief. When it was as if it were said, "Then where shall we be?", He said: ﴿Your abode﴾, that is, your dwelling, your residence and your gathering-place, ﴿is the Fire﴾, having no resting place for you other than it, burning you just as you used to burn the hearts of the friends of God by your pursuit of desires and your neglect of the rights of those in need. He confirmed this (p-278) by His saying: ﴿It is your master﴾, that is, none other than it, ﴿your companion and the place of your nearness, your destination and your helper, in the manner of "their greeting therein will be a painful blow"; so it is more fitting for you; you have no nearness to anything other than it, nor is anything other than it a master, nor a destination other than it, nor a helper except it. Since the implied meaning is: "Then it is an evil master," He followed it with His saying: ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾, that is, this Fire to which you have come.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 16:

Since this was a admonition that cures the sickness of hearts and removes the veil of distress, it produced His saying, urging them to turn toward His Book, which He showed mercy to His servants by sending down upon the tongue of His Prophet (ﷺ) in a manner that makes its inimitability (i'jaz) known, that it is speech that coaxes them toward His presence and restrains them from what some of them asked Salman (may Allah be pleased with him) about, namely that he should narrate to them from the Torah and the Gospel. So whenever they asked him about something, Allah, glorified is He, sent down a verse that restrains them with it and alerts them that this Qur'an contains [everything] that is sought, until He sent down this verse, restraining them with this great restraint, lest anyone suppose that the Qur'an is not sufficient. It also warns them by what befell the People of the Book through their turning away from their own Scripture. Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, one year after the Hijrah. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: Allah reproached the hearts of the believers at the end of thirteen years from the revelation of the Qur'an, so He said: ﴿Has the time not come?﴾ That is, has it not drawn near, arrived, and reached a limit, ﴿for those who believe﴾, that is, those who affirmed faith with their tongues, truthfully or falsely, ﴿that their hearts should humble themselves﴾, that is, that they should have a high rank in faith, by becoming soft, calm, submissive, lowly and tranquil, so that they turn away from the perishable and turn toward the enduring, ﴿to the remembrance of Allah﴾ (p-279), that is, the Supreme King, besides whom there is no good. Thus whoever was lying in his faith becomes truthful in it, and whoever was weak in religion becomes strong, so he does not seek for his religion a remedy, nor for his heart's sickness a cure, other than the Qur'an, for the remembrance of Allah polishes the rust of hearts and burnishes their mirrors.

Since remembrance alone is sufficient for humility, repentance and submission, because it gathers every desire and is the source of every awe, and since some people have no influence over what belongs to Him, glorified is He, of majesty and honour, He said: ﴿and what has come down﴾, that is, what Allah, exalted is He, has sent down gradually, according to the recitation of the majority (qira'at al-jama'ah) with the doubled letter (tashdid), and what has been found to be sent down from Allah upon the Seal of His Messengers (ﷺ), according to the recitation of Nafi' and Hafs from 'Asim, and of Ruways with a variant from him, from Ya'qub, with the lightened form (takhfif), ﴿of the truth﴾, that is, of promise, threat, admonition and other things, upon your Prophet (ﷺ), from the Qur'an, as an indication that other than this remembrance has been entered by intruders, whereas this one is established with a firmness that no one can remove.

Since competition and rivalry have a great effect in stirring the resolve of the proud and the people of high aims, He said: ﴿and let them not be like those who﴾. Since knowledge by itself is sufficient to raise resolve, how much more so when it comes from Allah, and how much more so when it comes in a Book, He alluded to this by using the passive form, saying: ﴿were given the Book﴾, that is, had it been from other than Allah, it would still have been worthy of guidance, so how much more so when it is from Him. Since the sending down of Books was only upon the Children of Israel (p-280), and therefore did not encompass all past time, He introduced the preposition, saying: ﴿before﴾, that is, before what was sent down to you, and they were the Jews and the Christians.

Since they were, at every moment, passing over, He said, coupling it to ﴿were given the Book﴾: ﴿and the term grew long for them﴾, that is, the time that We set for their nobility and extended for their exaltedness, from the beginning of their being given the Book, which by its nature softens hearts. The term (al-amad) is the appointed time, and each of the two is applied to the whole period and to its end, and likewise the limit (al-ghayah), according to the grammarians' statement: "min" is for the beginning of the limit and "ila" is for its end, while the intended meaning is the whole period. ﴿So their hearts hardened﴾, that is, through the length of time, ﴿their hearts﴾, that is, became hard and crooked, to the point that they were no longer responsive to acts of obedience and goodness. So at every moment they were in severe obstinacy toward their prophets, peace be upon them, asking them for proposals. As for after being given the Book, they went far in hardness, so they inclined toward the abode of turbidity with all their being, turned away from the abode of purity, and were drawn to destruction through following desires. Al-Qushayri said: hardness of heart arises only from following desire, and desire and purity do not come together.

Since the implied sense is: some of them remained firm while others wavered, He followed it with His saying: ﴿and many of them﴾, whose hardness had taken them out of religion altogether, root and branch, so they are ﴿defiantly disobedient﴾, that is, deeply immersed in the attribute of daring to step outside the circle of truth, which the Book had set as their boundary. On the authority of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, on the authority of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), that he said: "There was no interval between their Islam and the revelation of this verse, in which Allah rebukes them, except four years." Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir. Al-Haythami said: In its chain is Musa ibn Ya'qub al-Rabi'i, whom Ibn Ma'in and others declared trustworthy, while Ibn al-Madini declared him weak, and the rest of its narrators are narrators of the Sahih. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 17:

Since the greatest cause of hardness of heart is the denial of resurrection, and since the Arabs exceeded the People of the Book in the causes of hardness toward it, and since the conduct of one who acts in a way that indicates hardness is the conduct of one who denies it, He said, threatening them with it, confirming what the surah began with regarding the matter of giving life, alluding to the power to give life to hearts, presenting an example of removing hardness from them through polishing with remembrance and recitation, encouraging the continuation of that: ﴿Know﴾, that is, O you who have believed with your tongues, ﴿that Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King to whom belongs all perfection, so nothing can overpower Him, ﴿gives life﴾, that is, in a manner of renewal and continuity, as you witness, ﴿to the earth﴾ that is dry, ﴿with vegetation﴾. Since this description is established and constant, in actuality and in potential, and since the preposition here requires generality, He said: ﴿after its death﴾, without mentioning the preposition. Just as He gives it life, bringing forth vegetation from it after it had crumbled and become dust, so He gives life by gathering their bodies and pouring spirits into them, as He did with the vegetation, and as He did with the bodies the first time, equally, with no difference in any respect except that it is said: initiation is more difficult in custom. So beware of His might, fear His wrath, and hope for His mercy, for the giving of life to hearts, for He is able to give them life with the spirit of revelation, just as He gave life to the earth with the spirit of water, so that by their being given life through remembrance they become humble after their hardness, just as the earth became swelling after its humility and death through water.

When the matter was made utterly clear by this, it produced His saying: ﴿We have clarified﴾, that is, in accordance with what We possess of greatness. Since the Arabs understood from their language what others do not understand, they knew, from the inimitability of the Qur'an, through the abundance of its benefits, the grandeur of its aims, the subtlety of its methods, the magnitude of its perceptions, the eloquence of its compositions, the firmness of its styles, and other aspects of its affairs, its kinds and its arts, that which yields certainty that it is the speech of Allah, what others do not know; so it was as if they were specially addressed by this clarification. Thus He placed the preposition first and said: ﴿for you the signs﴾, that is, the illuminating indications. Since the context concerns resurrection, which is among the pillars of the foundations of religion, and since reason is sufficient in analogizing it to vegetation, and since an act that does not lead to the happiness of the Hereafter is deficient, and since reason that does not save its possessor is equal to non-existence, He said, expressing with the particle of postponement, unlike what preceded in Al 'Imran, since that concerns the interests of the soul which are hidden, and motives that call to understanding them and urge to mastering their knowledge: ﴿so that you may reason﴾, that is, so that you may be among those who know that and hear it from the creatures, in hope that reason may be attained by you through what is renewed for you of understanding it, by way of continual connection through persistence.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 18:

When charity was like the seed mentioned earlier, that God, exalted is He, brings it to life and multiplies it manifold, many times over, in proportion to the fertility of the land, He said, concluding from what has passed, informing (p-283) that among the greatest things that indicate the humility (khushu') that is urged, and the distance from the state of those who were given the Book in hardness of heart, is charity through spending, which He joined at its beginning with faith, and which He urged in many of its verses, as a warning that it is its fruit, which is not left behind by it, expressing it by what guides to the fact that it is the one who confirms its claim, and He emphasized it for those who doubt the Resurrection, against denying the blessing of charity, whether swiftly or later, bounding it to what is sensed: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity﴾, meaning, those who are firmly established in this attribute among the men, ﴿and the women who give charity﴾, meaning, among the women, with their wealth, to the weak whose giving indicates sincerity in faith, because the recipient is not hoped to bring any worldly benefit. Perhaps He merged them (adgham) as an indication of concealing charities. The reading of Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, with clear pronunciation (al-izhar), guides to increasing charity until it becomes apparent. The reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim with lightening (al-takhfif) indicates alongside that the confirming of faith, so each of the readings indicates both of them, and from the detail by mentioning the two categories, the intensity of the concern is known.

Since the form tafa''ala (taf'ul) indicates effort (takalluf), urging the bearing of the self toward adopting that until it becomes for it a character trait, in the utmost ease for it, He said, conjoining upon the relative clause's connection in the active participle, expressing with the past tense after conveying the attribute of constancy, indicating the occurrence of the action, conjoined upon [what], its implied sense being the placing of the masculine pronoun over the two categories by way of predominance: ﴿and those who lend to Allah﴾ (p-284), the One who possesses all perfection, by their confirmation, whether they are of the males or the females, and their spending in everything He has recommended spending upon. He emphasized and described it with His saying: ﴿a goodly loan﴾, meaning with the utmost of good-heartedness and sincerity of intention in charity and expenditure in the way of good. Its goodness is that one turns his gaze to the looking at his action, distinguishing himself by it and seeking a return for it. Al-Razi said: ﴿It will be multiplied﴾, meaning that loan, ﴿for them﴾, and they will be rewarded according to that multiplication, because He, to whom the loan is made, glory be to Him, is Forbearing and Generous, and He does not accept in goodness except with grace. He made it heavier in the reading of Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far [and Ya'qub], indicating intensity in multiplication, and He expressed it with the form mufa'alah in the reading of the community, to convey that that multiplication is something that must occur, and that He acts in it as one who competes with another and overcomes him. He built it for the passive, indicating the dazzling greatness, from which it necessarily follows that it is with utmost ease: ﴿and for them﴾, meaning, along with the multiplication, ﴿is a generous reward﴾, meaning, there is no turbidity in it through cessation, nor scarcity, nor any increase in any way whatsoever.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 19:

When Allah, glorified and exalted be He, had explained that charity is like the seed, which is among the finest and most delightful of profits, He explained what moves a person to it, encouraging it. He said, joining with the conjunction "wa" (and), indicating the firm establishment of all these attributes: ﴿And those who believe﴾, i.e., who bring this great reality into existence within themselves, ﴿in Allah﴾, i.e., the Supreme King to whom belong majesty and honour, ﴿and His messengers﴾, i.e., all of them, because of their connection to Him. So whoever denies something of [the messengers' teachings] concerning any one of them, or acts in the manner of one who denies him, has not truly believed in him. ﴿Those﴾, i.e., those who possess the lofty ranks and exalted stations, ﴿they are﴾, i.e., exclusively and not others, ﴿the truthful ones (al-siddiqun)﴾, i.e., those who are at the utmost degree of truthfulness and of affirming what whoever hears it ought to affirm. Al-Qushayri said: "The siddiq (truthful one) is one whose outward and inward are equal." It is also said: "He is the one who takes the matter by its most difficult course, does not descend to concessions, and does not need interpretations." Since the siddiq is not firmly established in the state of siddiqiyya except through being qualified for the rank of martyrdom (shahada), Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the martyrs (al-shuhada')﴾, expressed with a plural form whose singular is shahid, joined with "wa" to indicate the strength of establishment in each of the two attributes. [Al-Qushayri] said: They are those who witness with their hearts the inner realities of union and dwell with their secrets in the abodes of nearness. He magnified the matter further by His saying: ﴿with their Lord﴾, i.e., the One who has bestowed upon them, by nearness, [a rank like that] lofty rank of martyrdom, bearing witness to Allah for all that He sent His messengers and the earlier prophets with, over their peoples, and being present in all delights through martyrdom in the way of Allah. Mujahid said: "Every believer is a siddiq and a shahid," and he recited this verse. ﴿For them﴾, i.e., all of those, from among those who passed, who are described [with goodness], ﴿is their reward﴾, i.e., that which their Lord has made [for them], ﴿and their light﴾, [i.e.,] that which He has increased for them of His bounty by His mercy. Those are the companions of everlasting bliss.

When He mentioned the people of happiness, gathering all their categories, He followed them with the people of wretchedness, in order to contrast them. He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., who concealed what the lights of their intellects and the mirrors of their reflection pointed to, ﴿and denied Our signs﴾, despite their greatness through their being ascribed to Us, whether they were in that concealing or openly rejecting, or the knower acted in the manner of the denier. ﴿Those﴾, i.e., those cut off from good [exclusively], ﴿are the companions of the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim)﴾, i.e., the Fire which is at the utmost of its blazing, abiding therein from among the disobedient. As for others, their entering it, if they enter it, is not [in] the manner of companionship which indicates constancy. Those are the liars, to whom no testimony is accepted before their Lord; for them is their punishment, and upon them is their darkness. The verse is of al-ihtibak: it mentions first the siddiqiyya and what accompanies it, and then mentions its opposites second; and it mentions al-Jahim second as an indication of al-na'im first. Its secret is that the first is greater in honour, and the second is greater in humiliation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 20:

When [Allah, glorified is He] mentioned the condition of the two groups, the wretched and the happy, the matter of the Hereafter was thereby established, and they knew that it is the everlasting life, which has no end, either of honour or of humiliation. What makes one deserving of humiliation there is only the turning toward this world, because it is present, and the forgetting of the Hereafter, because it is absent. He said, drawing a conclusion from what came before and explaining the reality of what the obligated person, who is made to crave desire, is inclined to of the immediate world, by what He had cautioned against in it, beginning with what necessitates the utmost (p-287) alertness and presence: ﴿Know﴾, that is, O servants who are being tested. He emphasised the meaning by adding "mā" [for what] because of people's heedlessness regarding it, and said, restricting by a restriction of correction (qaṣr qalb): ﴿That the life of this world﴾, that is, the present one, which I have made desirable in asceticism toward it and departure from it through charity and the good loan, ﴿is only play﴾, that is, toil with no fruit, so it is vain, like the play of children, ﴿and amusement﴾, that is, something a person rejoices in, so that it diverts him and occupies him from what concerns him, then it passes away like the amusement of youths. Then He followed this with the greatness of what distracts in this world, and said: ﴿and adornment﴾, that is, something that delights the eye and gladdens the soul, like the adornment of women, and He followed it with its fruit and said: ﴿and boasting﴾, that is, like the boasting of rivals, some of them vaunting over others.

Since this was specific to the people of desires, He said: ﴿among you﴾, that is, it draws one to self-exaltation, which leads to envy and hatred. Then He followed that with what the boasting is achieved by, and said: ﴿and multiplying﴾, that is, from both sides, ﴿in wealth﴾, that is, which only a fool boasts of, since it is inclined to perish, ﴿and children﴾, in whom only a foolish person takes pride, since they are enemies. And all that has been mentioned is passing away, and the calamities of this world are dreadful, and it is only a trial and a test, through which the grateful is made to appear apart from others. Then, for all of that, it may be that its departure is near, so that it will be the opposite of what it was, and this is more severe in regret. The correspondence of this with what follows is that a person grows up in the lap of his guardian, then matures, grows strong, earns wealth and offspring, and people gather around him, so there occur among them admirable matters and diverting, delightful conditions. Then when his youth is complete, its coming and going extinguish it (p-288), and its forms and its peers, he begins to decline and does not cease until he grows grey, falls ill, weakens, and ages, and calamities, shocks, and afflictions befall him in his wealth, his body, his children, and his companions. Then at the end of all that he dies. So his affair has perished, and after a little while his mention is forgotten, and his wealth has become another's, and the adornment he enjoyed is enjoyed by others. So this world is contemptible, and more contemptible than it is the one who seeks it, and less worthy than it is the rivalry for it. It is nothing but a carcass, and the seekers of a carcass have no worth, and the basest of them is the one who is stingy with it. Al-Qushayri said: This blameworthy world is whatever occupies the servant away from the Hereafter, so everything that occupies him from the Hereafter is "the world", end of quotation.

When He, glorified is He, established that it is a passing shade and a dreadful accident, and some people awaken and give thanks while others become blind and disbelieve, and the second category was more numerous, because its existence and its coming toward a person blinds most hearts to its worthlessness, He struck a parable for this, establishing what preceded of its description, since parables have in establishing and depicting things what no other means has. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿Like the likeness﴾, that is, what I have mentioned of its matter resembles the likeness of ﴿rain﴾, that is, a downpour that came after drought [and] bad condition.

Since the parable is in the context of belittling the world and warning against it, He expressed the farmer in terms that repel, and said: ﴿which pleased the disbelievers﴾, that is, the cultivators, from whom there came the tilling and the sowing, which the tiller covers with his tilling, just as the disbeliever covers the reality of the lights of faith because of what arises from denial and transgression. The farmer's delight does not reach a limit [to] (p-289) which diverts from Allah unless it is accompanied by disbelief in Him, glorified is He, for the believer, even if this pleases him, is reminded thereby of the power of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and of His greatness, and of what He has prepared for the people of His obedience in the Hereafter, so that leads him to obedience. Thus the expression "disbelievers", which means cultivators, instead of the latter, is an indication of the greatness of that vegetation, for it does not please those who know it and who practise it, who are fully devoted to that craft, so rivalry in it is only what is extreme in pleasing.
