And it also indicates that nothing of the world pleases anyone with a pleasure that makes him incline and feel at ease with it, to a degree that leads to the diversion mentioned in the verse, and that is only due to disbelief within oneself, the least of which is ingratitude for blessing, which by its nature calls to remembrance of the Creator and to recollection of the beauty of gratitude, and abandoning gratitude is disbelief. ﴿Its vegetation﴾, that is, the vegetation of that rain, just as worldly expansion for the disbeliever, as a lure from Allah, mostly pleases the disbeliever in his disbelief.

Since the crop withers after a while and perishes, as is the case with the whole world, He said: ﴿Then it dries up﴾, that is, its movement quickens, so its drying completes, and its harvest becomes due, ﴿so you see it yellowed﴾, that is, after that, near it, in a state with neither fruit nor even vegetation. For this reason He spoke with the verb of being, because the context is for renunciation of the world and that it is a passing shade with no reality: ﴿Then﴾, that is, after its drying and whitening have reached their end, ﴿it becomes﴾, that is, a becoming as if it were stamped upon it. And He, glorified is He, went further in establishing its perishing by the use of the verb "kāna" (to be) here for emphasis, because the context is to establish (p-290) that the world is nothingness, even if it is at the height of abundance, coming and favourable, unlike what preceded in the Zumar. So He said: ﴿debris﴾, as if the state of being debris was in its nature and original constitution.

When He mentioned the passing shade, He mentioned its lasting and everlasting trace, dividing it into two categories, and said, conjoining it to what is implied: this is the condition of the world in the swiftness of its passing and the certainty of its annihilation and [perishing]: ﴿And in﴾, that is, what has deceived you of the condition of the world, and it is in ﴿the Hereafter﴾, one of two outcomes: ﴿a severe punishment﴾, that is, for whoever takes it without its right, turning away from the remembrance of Allah, because being deceived by it is what causes it, so it was as if he were it.

When He had put forward what is the most prevalent cause, because most of creation is lost, He followed it with the saved category, and said: ﴿And forgiveness﴾, that is, for the people of the first rank in faith, ﴿from Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, for whoever remembers, through what He did for him in the world, His greatness, glorified is He, and His majesty, and so repents of his sins and returns to Him for purification from his faults. ﴿And approval﴾ is for the people of the highest rank, who are those who turned toward Him, glorified is He, and gave thanks to Him as He deserves, by expending their utmost effort in what pleases Him. So the end of the verse is a division of the world in its reality, lest it be supposed from restricting it to what was mentioned at the beginning of the verse that it cannot be otherwise. The meaning is that what He mentioned first is the most prevalent of its conditions, and its outcome is the Fire, while whatever of it is faith, obedience, and reflection of tawhid for Allah, with glorification and knowledge leading to (p-291) taking it as provision and looking at it as reflection and worship, then it is the Hereafter, not the world. It has been established that the likeness of the rain mentioned is debris, and at times it is followed by lasting distress, and at other times by everlasting joy. So whoever works in this as the prudent farmer works, guards the crop from what harms it, harvests it at its time, does what is proper with it, and does not forget Allah's right in it, its outcome gladdens him and its end is praised. And whoever neglects that, [it brings him regret, and that is the parable of the world: whoever works in it by Allah's command, its debris brings him lasting joy, and whoever neglects that,] it bequeaths him constant sorrow. And just as the implication was: "So what is the Hereafter for one who strives for it while he is a believer, except a established truth and a thanked striving," He conjoined to it His saying: ﴿And what is the life of this world﴾, that is, because it occupies with its adornment while it is passing, ﴿except the enjoyment of delusion﴾, that is, a diversion in itself [delusion], having no reality except that, because it is not lawful for one who turns to enjoying it except that, since it does not gladden in proportion to what it harms.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 57, verse 21:

When he had shown that the world is an illusion and a fleeting thing, so as to turn the perfect among the servants away from it because of its lowliness and worthlessness, and that the Hereafter is lasting and perfect, so that they would desire it with the utmost desire and yearn for it with the fullest yearning because of its perfection, nobility and majesty, this produced His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Hasten﴾, that is, strive in seeking it through righteous deeds with the truest striving, like the one who races against a person: he exerts himself and strives with the utmost effort to outstrip him, though perhaps his companion is slow and so he goes at an easy pace. As for *al-musara'a* (hastening, a more intense form of racing), it is achieved only through exertion of the self on both sides together with speed according to custom. Therefore the verse of Al 'Imran, which commands *al-musara'a*, which is more specific than *al-musabaqa* (racing), is more eloquent, because it urges detachment from the self, from wealth and from all worldly portions entirely and fundamentally. For this reason its Garden is for the God-fearing who are described thus. As for this verse, it is in the context of *al-tasdiq* (affirmation of faith), which is detachment from the excesses of wealth. For this reason its [Garden] is for those who believed.

Since the station is great, and man, even with that effort, is weak, and it befits him only to be pardoned, whether he be among the foremost or the later ones among the righteous and the near-stationed, he drew attention to this by His saying concerning the foremost: ﴿to forgiveness﴾, that is, a covering over your sins, both in their substance and their effect, ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you, by having nurtured you and developed you after bringing you into being through various means, so that you perform the causes of that through obedience to His commands, glorified is He, and avoidance of His prohibitions. Since the intended purpose of forgiveness is what follows from it as a result, He said: ﴿and a Garden﴾, that is, a garden which, because of the greatness of its trees and the abundance of its rivers, covers whoever is within it. Since that cannot be complete without vastness, He said: ﴿whose breadth﴾, that is, then consider its length. Since the context, as he made clear, concerns detachment from the excesses of wealth only, because what is promised here is less than what is in Al 'Imran, He mentioned it singularly and explicitly stated the breadth, saying: ﴿is like the breadth of heaven and earth﴾, that is, were some of it joined to some. The verse of Al 'Imran allows for length, with all the heavens and the earth in their present form. It is also possible that this is on the assumption that each of the two is cut into pieces, and the head of each piece is joined to the head of the other, and all the pieces extend to their ends like a shoelace. This verse, on its apparent sense, is one breadth and one earth. ﴿It has been prepared﴾, that is, this promised Garden has been made ready and its affair completed in the easiest manner, ﴿for those who believed﴾, that is, who have actualized this truth in a way free of doubt, even at the lowest level, so they are among the foremost. This indicates that the Garden now exists, in many verses, and that faith suffices for entitlement to it, and the hadiths of intercession support this. ﴿In God﴾, that is, the One who possesses all greatness in His own essence, sincerely believing in Him, ﴿and His messengers﴾, so they do not make a distinction between any of them. This Garden is not mentioned in Al 'Imran. If it is said that "heaven" here is generic because the context concerns the *siddiqun* (the truthful) and the martyrs, it was more eloquent in that case to state the plural and not state the breadth, because it occurs in a context in which striving (*jihad*) is explicitly mentioned. The divine custom has been to glorify the strivers, because of the severity of the danger concerning the self and the difficulty of departing from it and from all beloved things.

Since what was mentioned of the promise of forgiveness and the Garden is great, especially for one who believes even if his faith is at the highest degrees and with complete freedom from all works, He magnified it by His saying, in response to those who would oblige Him, glorified is He, to give some reward or punishment: ﴿That﴾, that is, the matter, which is very great, ﴿is the bounty of God﴾, that is, the King to whom there is no equal, so there is no objection to Him, ﴿He gives it to whomever He wills﴾. Perhaps the expression with the present tense indicates that this is specific to this community, which has fewer deeds and greater reward. Therefore, when the People of the Book envied them, Exalted is He said: Have I wronged you in anything of your affair? When they say: No, because the reward distributed among all the groups is according to the stipulated condition, He says: That is My bounty; I give it to whom I will.

﴿And God﴾, that is, and the state is that the King, singled out with all the attributes of perfection, to Him belongs the whole affair, ﴿is the Possessor of Mighty Bounty﴾, that is, the One who is exalted above having minds encompass His description.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 22:

When the world (al-dunya) was preventing one from devoting oneself to the Hereafter through its pleasures and bounties, and it was, just as it is a abode of ease, also the abode of [trial], and He, glory be to Him, had limited Himself in the preceding verse to the first, because the context concerns spending (infaq) and encouraging the lofty qualities of character, and making the race toward felicity the result of renouncing the world, the soul became moved to ask about what hinders one from good through being struck with the whips of trial. So He said, consoling them about it, because souls are more affected by what is disliked and more quickly stirred by blows, and confirming and inspiring by informing them that there was no good or evil in it except by a decree that was determined in pre-eternity and a measure that was made firm and became obligatory when nothing else existed, He, Mighty and Majestic. He mentioned the feminine verb, which may also be masculine, because the feminine is not a true feminine, as an indication of the great impact of evil: ﴿ma asaba﴾ ("no affliction has befallen"). He emphasized the negation and said: ﴿min musibatin﴾ ("of any affliction"), which in origin applies to everything that comes, whether good or evil, except that common usage restricted it to evil. He included both the settled and the moving by His words: ﴿fi al-ard﴾ ("on the earth"), that is, from its plants, its waters, and the like; ﴿wa la fi anfusikum﴾ ("nor in yourselves"), [that is,] by death, sickness, the evil eye, and accidents; ﴿illa﴾ (except that) it exists ﴿fi kitab﴾ ("in a Book"), that is, written, because it is predestined and completed from eternity. He made clear that the writing occurred after He, glory be to Him, existed with nothing beside Him, by introducing the preposition, so He said: ﴿min qabli an nabra'ahā﴾ ("before We bring it into being"), that is, before We create, originate, and decree the affliction, the earth, and the souls. This is evidence that the acquisitions of the servants are created and decreed by Him, glory be to Him.

Since that is difficult for the created being, and it is the thing most disliked by him, standing with illusion, He said, emphasizing: ﴿inna dhalika﴾ ("indeed, that") — that is, the great matter, which is His knowledge of the thing and His writing of it in its details before its existence, then His driving of souls and causes to bring it out after its creation according to the measure of what His knowledge and writing had preceded — ﴿ʿala Allah﴾ ("for Allah") — that is, given His comprehensive perfection — ﴿yasir﴾ ("is easy"), because His knowledge encompasses everything and His power is all-encompassing, nothing overcoming it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 23:

When He had made clear this great matter, which indicates what belongs to Him, glorified is He, of majesty and greatness, He made clear the fruit of His actions by His saying: ﴿So that you do not despair﴾. That is, We have informed you that, by virtue of the greatness that is Ours, We have finished with the decree, so nothing in it can be imagined to be advanced, delayed, altered or changed, because grief does not repel it, nor does joy bring it about or gather it. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Mu'adh, let your worry lessen; what is decreed will come to pass." So that you do not ﴿grieve﴾, that is, do not grieve a great and excessive grief ﴿over﴾ [what is] in the原 basic nature (al-jibillah), which reaches its limit by pursuing its causes and persisting in them, so that anger and dissatisfaction with the decree result from it, and perhaps this drags one to a grave matter ﴿that has escaped you﴾ of worldly beloved things, ﴿nor rejoice﴾, that is, be gladdened with a gladness that leads to exultation by persisting in it, along with [what is] in the basic nature ﴿in what He has given you﴾, that is, what has come to you of it, according to the reading of Abu 'Amr with the short vowel (al-qasr: ﴿ātākum﴾ as "has come to you"), and "has given you [Allah]" according to the reading of the rest with the long vowel (al-madd). This indicates that blessings, in both their coming into being and their continuance, necessarily require a guardian. Moreover, if they were left to themselves, they would perish, because by their own essence there is nothing but non-existence. He, glorified is He, has made clear that in this His decree and His writing there is a secret: whoever prepares his soul to lose what is in his possession, whether of substances or meanings, before He commands him to non-existence and to finding, that will not divert him from the aforementioned race. So what is forbidden is persisting in grief until one departs from patience, and in joy until it distracts from gratitude, not the basic meaning itself, because it is not among voluntary actions. Ja'far al-Sadiq said: "Why do you grieve over what is lost, when loss does not return it to you? And why do you rejoice in existence, when death does not leave it in your hand?" - End. God has consoled the believers, out of mercy towards them in their afflictions, and made them renounce their desires, by informing them that their regret over the loss of what is sought does not restore it, and their joy at the attainment of what is loved does not benefit them, and because there is no hope of its remaining except by storing it with God. This is achieved by saying at a calamity: "God has decreed, and what God willed He did," and in blessing: "Thus He decreed," and "I do not know what its like is":

﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I am grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Naml: 40]. So he remains fearful at the time of affliction, hoping for the trace of blessing, saying in both states: "What God willed came to be, and what He did not will did not come to be." More perfect than this is that he be delighted by the remembrance of his Lord towards him in both states, as the poet [said]:

"Water for your abode, which, had it not been, my heart would not have been an abode for passion."

This is the attribute of those who are freed from the bondage of the soul, and the worth of men is known only by the changing occurrences. Whoever is not altered by harms and is not affected by pleasures, he is the master of his time; al-Qushayri indicated this. Since excessive pursuit of sorrow arises only from despair and forgetfulness of blessings, and excessive joy that leads to exultation is drawn only by arrogance and exultation, and boasting was among the qualities of the people of this world, He, Exalted, said, explaining that what was forbidden earlier was persisting with the disposition in grief and joy, adding to what is implied: "Indeed God does not love every self-deceiving ingrate" ﴿Indeed God does not love﴾, that is, He does not act as one who loves, by honouring ﴿every arrogant﴾, that is, every proud one who looks at what is in his hand of this world, ﴿boastful﴾. Al-Qushayri said: arrogance is among the remnants of the self and its seeing itself, and boasting [is from] seeing the importance of what one boasts of.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 24:

Since greed (al-bukhl) is among the attributes of the arrogant one who boasts of wealth, and since the urging to spend (al-infaq) had already been mentioned, and since the pleasure of pride and self-conceit (al-fakhar wa'l-ikhtiyal), to which wealth has led him, is what drives him to stinginess out of fear of poverty (al-iqtar), which entails lowliness (al-sighar) in the eyes of the people of this world, Allah the Exalted says, describing the arrogant one or everyone: ﴿Those who are stingy﴾, meaning they bring this reality into being continuously; ﴿and enjoin upon people﴾, meaning everyone they know, ﴿stinginess﴾, intending that they have companions who act upon their vile deeds and defend them; or that by their deeds of arrogance and insolence regarding the wealth which stinginess has gained for them, they prompt God to lead them, by way of gradual enticement (istidraj), to the stinginess of others, because when others see them magnified through wealth, they become stingy so that their wealth may increase and they may be magnified. All of this is the result of their exultation in what they possess and their insolence when they attain it; so they were enjoiners of stinginess inasmuch as they were its causes, and a cause is like one who commands in bringing a thing into existence.

Since the implied sense is: "Whoever turns to what has been recommended (ila ma nudiba [ilayhi]) of goodly lending, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, then Allah is Most Appreciative (Shakur), Forbearing (Halim)," He joined to it [His saying], censuring stinginess and warning against it: ﴿And whoever turns away﴾, meaning he imposes upon himself [of] aversion contrary to what is in his nature of love of goodness and turning toward Allah; ﴿then indeed Allah﴾, meaning He to whom belong all attributes of perfection, ﴿He is﴾, meaning alone, ﴿the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani)﴾, meaning free of His wealth and its expenditure, while everything is in need of Allah; ﴿the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid)﴾, meaning the One deserving of praise, whether or not those who praise Him do so. The reading of Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, with the omission of [huwa], conveys the restriction of the subject to the predicate by way of definiteness (li'l-ta'rif), although the reading of the majority is more emphatic (akkad).

(p. 299) When the proofs became manifest, so that no one had any excuse left, and their light spread until it filled the created realms and rose to such a height that Saturn (Kiwan) was dwarfed beneath its loftiness, and when what preceded had explained the outcome of this world and the reality of its nature, and that the human being, when left to himself, commits what is unbecoming, such as boasting and the like, and abandons what is intended for him of the good to which he was called, out of ignorance and from submission to his nature, and when the closing of the previous verse might have given the impression of partnership, God the Exalted said, negating that in response to one who expected information about the rest of the prophets: "They were given of clarity what removed confusion." This confirms the removal of excuse by establishing proofs through sending the messengers with present miracles and enduring books, informing that whoever turns away is obliged to be brought to submission by the sword. For the Wise, the Mighty, His greatness and wisdom refuse to leave the one who turns away without a clear proof that turns him back from what he is in, and without compulsion that restrains him from what makes him transgress. He says: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers﴾, meaning with what We possess of greatness, ﴿Our messengers﴾, meaning those who have the utmost of honour through their connection to Us, from the angels to the prophets, upon all of them be the most excellent blessings, peace, [greetings] and honour, and from the prophets to the nations, ﴿with clear proofs﴾, meaning those that necessitate submission immediately, because there is no confusion in them at all. The text indicates the greatness of His prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, in that, because of the elevation of their stations through being sent, it is as though they came to the servants from a very high place. So He said: ﴿And We sent down﴾ with Our greatness (p. 300), than which nothing is higher, ﴿with them the Book﴾, meaning the one that preserves, for the time of receiving, in the rulings and laws.

Since understanding the Book may be difficult, it requires a polished mind, lengthy reflection, great patience and abundant knowledge. Al-Razi said: "It was said for this reason: Were it not for the Book, the intellect would be bewildered, and were it not for the intellect, the Book would not benefit." He followed this with what both the great and the small, the ignorant and the expert, share in knowing, and which is the closest of things to the Book in knowledge, by correspondence of reality to what is intended. So He said: ﴿and the Balance﴾, meaning justice and wisdom. Perhaps it is every means by which measurement occurs, sensory or abstract. Its being mentioned after the Book indicates that its not deviating is due to the absence of self-interest and the like, so whoever takes the Book as judge, free from self-interest, reaches the goal. ﴿So that people may establish﴾, meaning those among whom there is the capacity to move toward all lofty things, ﴿justice﴾, meaning the justice beyond which there is nothing more, so that all their conditions are well ordered. This is for whoever submits to the clear proofs, either for the sake of the one who established them or out of desire for them in his sight.

Since turning away after clear explanation necessitates repelling corruption by various kinds of struggle, He said, threatening and bestowing favour, encouraging and warning, and expressing the creation by "sending down" as honour and exaltation: ﴿And We sent down﴾, meaning We created a great creation by what We possess of power, ﴿iron﴾, meaning that known in a form of strength, hardness, (p. 301) softness and sharpness, fit to receive impression. It is reckoned as though it came down from what is in the earth. Therefore its bringing into being was called "sending down". Also, the commands for bringing into being and annihilation descend from the heaven through the hands of the angels, because the heaven is the place of great events, marvels and secrets, since water, which is its origin and the origin of every growing thing, descends from the heaven, and the earth is for it like the womb for the drop.

Since there was longing to know the cause of its sending down, He said: ﴿In it is severe might﴾, meaning strength, vigour and punishment, ﴿severe﴾, because of its hardness suited to keenness and sharpness, ﴿and benefits for people﴾, through what is made from it of their utilities and aids, so that their conditions may be sustained by it. Al-Baydawi said: "There is no craft except that iron is its instrument." Since the intended meaning was: that God may know who disobeys Him and forsakes His friends, by placing His might in what He did not command, in support of his devil and his desire and his seduction, He joined to it His saying: ﴿And that God may know﴾, meaning the One to whom belongs all greatness, knowledge of witnessing, for the sake of establishing proof by what suits the intellects of creatures, so that the reward is for action and not for knowledge. He placed the pronoun of religion [upon Him], glorified be He, exalting Him because He is its legislator. So He said: ﴿who helps Him﴾, meaning who strives earnestly to persist in supporting His religion, ﴿and His messengers﴾, by defending them and calling to them, that help being ﴿in the unseen﴾ of promise and threat, [meaning] because the helper affirms what is absent from him of that, or being absent from everything that made support obligatory for him. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "They help Him and do not see Him." End of quotation. In this verse God left no excuse for anyone regarding the messengers, who are the human kind, supported by what removes confusion from them, and the Book, exalted above the speech of creatures, and the intellect that knows justice, and the weapon that repels the ignorant. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"I was sent before the Hour with the sword." So the explanation of the laws is by the Book, the straightening of the doors of justice is by the Balance, and the execution of these meanings is by the sword, for the interests of religion cannot be safeguarded without the awe of authority. The king and religion are twins: religion without a king is lost, and a king without religion is void. The sultan is the shadow of God on earth. The outward meanings of the Book are for the common folk, and the weighing of its knowledge for the people of realities is by the Balance. Whoever goes out of the two groups, for him there is iron, which is the sword, because the disturbance of religion comes from him. Al-Razi drew attention to this.

Since seeking help is a likely cause of suspecting weakness, He said, negating that, emphasizing it to cut off the obstinacy of the obstinate, and manifesting the Greatest Name to indicate that whoever possesses all the attributes of perfection cannot be touched by need: ﴿Indeed God﴾, meaning the One to whom all greatness belongs. Since there was no call here for more than this emphasis, unlike what was alluded to regarding the expulsion from the homes mentioned in the pilgrimage and the like, He said, informing that He is free of need from everything, and stripping the predicate of the lam: ﴿is Strong﴾, meaning He is capable (p. 303) of destroying all His enemies and supporting whoever helps Him from His friends, ﴿Mighty﴾, so He is not in need of anyone's help. He only called His servants to support His religion so that He might establish proof against them, so that He may show mercy to whom He wills by their compliance with what is commanded, and punish whom He wills by committing what is forbidden, by His construction of this abode upon the wisdom of linking causes to means.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 26:

When He generalized the messengers, gathering them together in the clear signs, the listener was bound to expect a specification. He singled out from among them two of the steadfast messengers (ulu al-'azm), two fathers who combine in offspring and in messengership, because that is more fitting to the purpose of the surah, which is to make clear the excellence of Muhammad (ﷺ), whose messengership extended in a generality that was not given to anyone else. Nuh (peace be upon him) was sent to the people of the earth because they were of one tongue. The generality of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was through his offspring (peace be upon them). After the two of them, He specified 'Isa (peace be upon him), with his messengership's generality to the Children of Israel through abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by another) and legislation. Then, through his descent upon this community, [he is mentioned] through confirmation and renewal. So He said: ﴿And We certainly sent﴾, that is, with what We possess of the attributes of perfection, beauty and majesty, ﴿Nuh﴾, the second father, and We made the predominant aspect of his messengership the manifestation of majesty; ﴿and Ibrahim﴾, father of the Arabs, the Romans and the Children of Israel, most of whose prophets are from his lineage, and We made the predominant aspect of his messengership the place of manifestation of honor. ﴿And We placed﴾, with what We possess of greatness, ﴿in their offspring prophethood﴾, which requires connection to the Supreme King for executing commands, (p-304) ﴿and the Book﴾, comprehensive of the rulings and governing the laws, by appointing prophets from among their offspring and sending down Books to them. So there is no prophet and no book except that it traces back to these two through the strongest of causes and the most exalted of lineages.

Since the manifestation of greatness requires the wretchedness of whomever He wills to be made wretched, with no regard for him, whoever he may be, whether he is connected to the friends or to the enemies, lest anyone feel secure and fall into loss, or anyone despair and be subjected to humiliation, [He said: ﴿So among them﴾, that is, among the offspring of these two categories, ﴿is one who is guided﴾, who is by the very gaze of Our good pleasure -] and he is the one who adheres to the path of the chosen ones, holds fast to their covenant, and does not deviate at all, even if he is from the descendants of the enemies.

Since whoever deviates after being reminded through the Books and the messengers deserves the utmost blame, even if he is one person, how much more so if they are many, He, by changing the context, drew attention to this and to the fact that the predominant condition is misguidance. So He said: ﴿And many of them﴾, that is, of the offspring described, ﴿are defiantly disobedient﴾, who are by the very gaze of wrath, even if they are the offspring of the chosen ones. They are those who opposed the friends through hostility, or innovation, or deviation from their way by adopting what they did not follow, through negligence or excess.

(p. 305) Since one of the great aims of this surah is to announce that all previous laws have been abrogated (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by a later one) by the law of this Prophet, whose message is comprehensive and universal for all creatures (ﷺ), He said, indicating the greatness of the sending and of the messengers by the particle of delay: (p. 305) ﴿Then We sent, following in their footsteps,﴾ meaning: with what We possess of greatness, a following-up whose greatness is beyond description, ﴿on their traces﴾ meaning the two parents mentioned and those messengers who passed before them. The pronoun does not return to "the offspring" (dhurriyya), because it remains with the messengers and after them. ﴿Our messengers﴾ meaning: We sent them one after another, among countless people of disbelievers, protected from them for the most part by what greatness requires. We did not bring the trace of the first of them to an end until We sent the one after him at his heels. [So every messenger is before the one who follows him, and those who come after him are behind him.] Thus each one follows up on him, because the first is going toward God and the second is following him. So our Prophet (ﷺ) is the most exalted of people in this attribute, because there is no prophet after him, and for this reason "the one who follows up" (al-muqaffi) was one of his names.

Since ʿIsa (peace be upon him) was the greatest of those who came after Musa (peace be upon him) from the Children of Israel, he abrogated his law, and this final Prophet (ﷺ) was strengthened by him in renewing his religion and confirming his law. Asceticism, tenderness and mercy were most evident among his followers, though this did not prevent them from a harshness that was noted earlier, on the basis that the cause of it was the long duration of time, which resulted in turning away from the present signs with him and the Book that remains after him. He singled him out for mention and repeated the governing verb, saying: ﴿And We sent after them﴾ meaning: We followed up, with what We possess of greatness, on their traces before they became obliterated, ﴿ʿIsa son of Maryam﴾, who was the last of those before the final Prophet, upon them be prayers and peace. Thus his community was the first of the nations commanded to follow him (ﷺ). ﴿And We gave him﴾ with what We possess of greatness (p. 306) ﴿the Gospel﴾, a book that preserves what he brought, establishes his religion, makes clear the Resurrection, gives good news of the Arab Prophet, clarifies his matter, and frequently mentions him. ﴿And We placed﴾ by Our might ﴿in the hearts of those who followed him﴾ meaning: with the utmost of their effort, so they conformed to his ways, ﴿compassion﴾ meaning: greater tenderness toward those who had a connection with them, ﴿and mercy﴾ meaning: tenderness and kindness toward those who had no cause of relation with them. Just as the Companions (may God be pleased with them) were merciful among themselves, so that they were humble toward the believers, though their hearts were extremely firm, and they were mighty against the disbelievers. The arrangement of the two attributes in this way is the strongest evidence that they were not intended for the sake of observing rhyming endings (fawasil) in "compassionate, merciful," as some exegetes said. It was mentioned at the end of Bara'a (Surah al-Tawba) that this is an opinion one may neither endorse nor rely upon, even if someone said it. ﴿And monasticism﴾ meaning: practices that lead to monkhood (rahbaniyya), adopting its appearance, and acting according to its rules, with exaggeration in worship, discipline, and withdrawal from people.

Since he placed the object before a verb not mentioned, so that it would be indicated by what explains it, in order that it be mentioned twice for emphasis, conveying the blame of innovation itself, he followed it with the explaining verb, saying: ﴿they invented it﴾ meaning: they made themselves bear the burden of practicing it and binding themselves to it, without having any precedent for it that they knew of, or that it was stated in His Book, although its aims do not reject it. For its sake they isolated themselves from people and secluded themselves in the mountains for companionship. Reports of them were widespread in the regions and the cities. In placing it before the verb there is another secret: it is fit to be coordinated with what precedes, so that one would not suppose in the word "invention" that God had no role in it. ﴿We did not prescribe it﴾ meaning: We did not make it obligatory [by Our greatness] ﴿for them﴾ in their Book, nor [upon] the tongue of their messenger. ﴿Except﴾ meaning: [but] they invented it ﴿seeking﴾ meaning: for the sake of imposing upon themselves the striving with utmost effort to purify hearts, refine souls, and purify deeds, ﴿the pleasure of God﴾ meaning: the great good pleasure of the Greatest King. He treated the disconnected exception as though it were connected, indicating that it is among what pleases God, and that He did not impose it upon them except out of mercy for them because of its difficulty, and that after they bound themselves to it He made it like the prescribed obligation. The meaning then is: "except so that they might seek His pleasure in a manner of steadfastness and permanence." The Imam Abu al-Qasim ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn [ʿAbd] al-Hakam al-Misri said in his book "The Conquests of Egypt and the Maghrib": When God, Mighty and Majestic, drowned Pharaoh and his armies, as Hani' ibn al-Mutawakkil narrated to us from Ibn Lahi'a from Yazid ibn Abi Habib from Tubayʿ, who said: Those of the sorcerers who had believed asked Musa (peace be upon him) for permission to return to their families and property in Egypt. He permitted them and prayed for them. They then lived as ascetics along with the mountaintops, and they were the first to practice asceticism. They were called the Shiʿa. A group of them remained with Musa (peace be upon him) until God, Mighty and Majestic, took him. Then monasticism ceased after them, until the companions of the Messiah (peace be upon him) afterward invented it.

Since its difficulty caused them to neglect it, by falling short of its requirements and sinking below its heights, He said: ﴿but they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾ meaning: they all kept it with the care of one who is anxious about its loss, ﴿with its proper observance﴾, by guarding with diligence the observance of deeds, states, and words. The guarding of deeds is to multiply them while belittling them, without looking at them. The observance of states is to strive while the state is still a claim. The observance of time is to stand with presence upon the carpet of witnessing the Majesty. This was mentioned by al-Razi. Rather, the attributes of humans prevailed over them, so some of them fell short of the high reach of it and sank below its lofty peaks. This is a great warning against innovations, a strong urging to adhere to what God has established and legislated, and a warning against excessive rigor, for no one overburdens the religion without being overcome by it. Traveling to innovation is exactly that. For this reason, leaving the religion through incarnation and union and other trials became frequent among the people of monasticism. Even if one appears to show that severity and excessive depth are good, because the Lawgiver, who encompasses knowledge of what no one else encompasses, forbade it, and experience has shown that it can deceive, since these people invented what they intended as good, it became a call for many of them to the abode of perdition. There is also in this a great urging to persist in the righteous deeds one is accustomed to, especially since the Prophet (ﷺ) did no deed except that he persisted in it, and he forbade (p. 309) excessive depth in religion, and commanded gentleness and moderation.

Since pursuing the self into excess in negligence may lead to leaving the religion, which entails disbelief and brings total destruction, He pointed to this by His saying: ﴿So We gave those who believed﴾ meaning: by what We possess of the attributes of perfection, ﴿those who believed﴾ meaning: who persisted in complete faith. Perhaps in the expression by the past tense after intending generality for the lower and higher is an indication that one who goes to extremes between faith and disbelief is not simply disobedient, as the ending of the verse indicates. So it is in the utmost condemnation of excessive depth and in praise of moderation. ﴿from among them﴾ meaning: from among these innovators, because they observed it with its proper observance and joined their faith in ʿIsa and those before him (upon them be prayers and peace) with their faith in Muhammad (ﷺ), whom he called to, the departure from the self, which is the spirit of monasticism, by agreeing with what is in their Book of the good news about him. ﴿Their reward﴾ meaning: what befits them, which is the multiplied pleasure of God.

Since following desires produces blameworthy attributes that become firmly rooted habits of the souls, He indicated this by shifting from the first course, saying: ﴿But many of them﴾ meaning: those who invented it and thereby wasted it, ﴿are defiantly disobedient﴾ meaning: deeply immersed in the attribute of going beyond the limits that God Most High has set. Al-Baghawi related, through the chain of al-Tha'labi, from Ibn Mas'ud (may God be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever believes in me has observed it [with its proper observance], and whoever does not believe in me, those are the ruined." End of quotation. Similar to this monasticism, in that the foundations of the religion do not reject it, is what some scholars understand from the Book and the Sunnah and then recall. So our taking it is from the principles he indicated, not from it itself. Just as the Companions (may God Most High be pleased with them) used to do things, and if the Prophet (ﷺ) approved of them, they became law for us, and we took them from his explanation (ﷺ), not from them. For whoever God has granted the rank of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) in some matter, and enabled him with its principles, and his ijtihad led him to the view that this is recommended and desirable, for example, that is by what the foundations of the religion attest to for him, and it stands in the position of what the Companions (may God be pleased with them) said, and the Prophet (ﷺ) approved. There is no difference between the Prophet (ﷺ) himself confirming it and its confirmation by the principles of his law. Whenever it is confirmed by the principles of his law, his command applies to it. Whenever it is not confirmed by them, it is among what his command does not apply to, and it is a rejection of its speaker. This is the distinction between good innovations and bad innovations. God is the Granter of success. Ibn Burjan mentioned the application of this hadith in which it says: "You will certainly follow the ways of those before you," and he noted that the companions of ʿIsa (peace be upon him) acted after him according to the Gospel until a king arose among them who altered their book, and Rome and Greece supported him in that. The people of faith became weak, and they were humiliated until they fled to the deserts, built hermitages, and invented monasticism. Likewise this occurred in this community, confirming the noble hadith. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) died, his successors followed him with excellence. When the rightly guided caliphate passed, trials accumulated as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had foretold, and the affliction intensified upon those who held firmly to clear faith. The Ancient House was stoned with catapult stones and demolished. ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr (may God be pleased with them both) was killed, and the city of the Prophet (ﷺ) was plundered for three days, and the best of its people were killed. So the Muslims considered seclusion obligatory, and they adhered to the zawiyas (lodges) and mosques, built ribats (frontier fortresses) on the shores of the sea, took up jihad against the enemy and the self, worked on purifying their morals, and adhered to poverty, taking as a model the condition of the People of the Bench (Ahl al-Suffa). They called themselves Sufis and spoke about scrupulousness (wara'), truthfulness, stations (manazil), states (ahwal), and spiritual ranks (maqamat). These people are the counterparts of those. God is the Granter of success.

**[Mention of the wisdom in the Injil (the Gospel) that calls for renunciation of this world and turning to God, which the adherents of this monastic path may rightly hold to]**

Matthew and others said, and the context mostly follows Matthew: "If your brother wrongs you, go and reprove him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen, take with you one or two more, for by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word will be established. And if he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church (al-bay'ah). And if he refuses to listen even to the church, let him be to you as a gentile (wathaniy) and a tax collector (ʿashshar). Truly I tell you..."

Luke said: "Take heed [now]. If your brother wrongs you, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him. And if he wrongs you seven times in a day and returns to you seven times saying, 'I repent,' forgive him."

Matthew said: "Then Peter came to him and said, 'If my brother wrongs me, how many times must I forgive him? Seven times?' He said, 'I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times.'"

For this reason the Kingdom of Heaven (malakut al-samawat) is likened to a king who wished to reckon with his servants. When he began the reckoning, one servant was brought before him who owed him a great sum (wiz'at), and he had nothing with which to repay. So his lord ordered that he be sold, with his wife, his children, and all that he had, until the debt was paid. That servant fell down prostrate [before him], saying, "O Lord, have patience with me, and I will repay you all." His lord had compassion on him, and released him from all that he owed.

That servant went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred dinars. He seized him, choked him, and said, "Pay me what you owe." That servant fell at his feet and begged [him], saying, "Have patience with me, and I will repay you." But he refused and went away, and cast him into prison until he should pay the debt. When the other servants saw this, they were greatly grieved [and] informed their lord of all that had happened. Then his lord summoned him and said to him, "You wicked servant! I forgave you all that you owed because you asked me. Should you not have shown mercy to your fellow servant as I showed mercy to you?" His lord was angry and handed him over to the tormentors until he paid all that he owed. "Thus will my heavenly Father do to you if you do not forgive your brothers their wrongs from your hearts."

When Jesus (Yasu') finished these words, he departed from Galilee and came to the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan, and a great crowd followed him, and he healed them there.

Luke said: "When the days of his ascension were complete, he set his face toward Jerusalem, and he sent messengers ahead of him. They went and entered a village of the Samaritans to prepare for him, but they did not receive him. His two disciples, James and John, said, 'O Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and destroy them, as Elijah (Ilya) did?' But he turned and rebuked them, saying, 'You do not know what spirit you are of. The Son of Man did not come to destroy the lives of people but to save them.' And he went on to another village."

Matthew said: "Then children were brought to him so that he might lay his hands on them and bless them, but the disciples rebuked them. Jesus said to them, 'Let the children come to me, and do not prevent them, for the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to such as these.' He laid his hands on them and blessed them."

Mark said: "Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive the Kingdom of God like a child will not enter it." He embraced them, laid his hands on them, and blessed them.

Matthew said: "He departed from there, and someone came to him and said, 'Good teacher' (Mark said: 'O good teacher'), what good must I do to inherit eternal life?" He said to him, "Why do you call me good? None is good but God alone. If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments." He said, "Which ones?" Jesus said: "Do not kill, do not steal, do not commit adultery, do not bear false witness." Mark said: "Do not defraud; honour your father and your mother; love your neighbour as yourself." The young man said to him, "I have kept all of these since my youth." Jesus said to him, "If you wish to be perfect, go." Mark said: "[Jesus looked at him and loved him, and said: 'You wish to be perfect'], one thing remains for you: go, sell everything you have and give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me." When the young man heard these words, he went away sorrowful, for he had great wealth.

Then Jesus said to his disciples: "Truly I tell you [that] it is hard for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of Heaven. And again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of Heaven." When the disciples heard this, they were utterly astonished and said, "Who then can be saved?" Jesus looked at them and said, "With people this is impossible, but with God all things are possible."

Then Peter answered and said to him, "Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what then will we have?" Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly I tell you: you who have followed me, in the new age (al-jabal al-atī), when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory, you will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of the children of Israel. Everyone who has left children, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or house, or field for my name's sake will receive a hundredfold and inherit eternal life."

Luke said: "There is no one who has left a home, or parents, or brothers, or a wife, or wealth for the sake of the Kingdom of God, but he will receive many times more in this age and in the age to come, eternal life." Matthew and others said: "Many who are first will be last, and the last will be first. The Kingdom of Heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard, and he agreed with the workers for a dinar a day..." — to the end of what passed in the A'raf (the Gospel sections) concerning the good news of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), in the parable of the labourers in the vineyard, where the last is preferred, namely the one who worked a little, over the one who worked more of the day. Ibn Burjan (ibn Burjān) has transmitted this from the Gospel at the end of his commentary on Surat al-Hadid in other words, a great deal of his wording differing from the version from which I quoted that. So I wished to mention Ibn Burjan's wording here to complete the benefit. He said: "In the book which is said to be the Gospel: 'Often the last will precede the first, and the first will be the stragglers of the last. For this reason the Kingdom of Heaven is likened to a wealthy man who went out to hire helpers to dig a vineyard at the beginning of the day, and he paid each one for his day a dirham. Then he brought them into his vineyard. When it was the third hour, he saw others in the marketplace with nothing to do, and he said, "Go you also to the vineyard, and I will give you your due." They went. He did the same at the sixth and the ninth hour. When it was the eleventh hour, he found others standing, and he said to them, "Why have you stood here all day without work?" They said, "No one has hired us." He said, "Go you, and I will give you your due." When the day ended, he said to his steward, "Call the workers, give them their wages, and begin with the last until you reach the first." He began with those who had come at the eleventh hour, and gave each one a dirham. The first came forward, those who had hoped for more, and he gave each of them a dirham. They complained about this to the owner of the vineyard, saying, "You have made us equal to those who worked only one hour of the day, while we have toiled all day and suffered its heat." He answered one of them and said, "I do not wrong you, friend. Did you not agree with me for a dirham? Take your due and go. It is my right to give the other what I gave you. Is it not lawful for me to do so? If you are envious, I am merciful." For this reason the last precede the first, and the first become the stragglers of the last. For the called are many, and the chosen are few.'"

Ibn Burjan mentioned that the sixth hour was for Jesus (ʿIsa) peace be upon him and his companions at the beginning of the matter, and the ninth hour was for Muhammad (ﷺ), and the eleventh hour was for the end of time, as if he meant the days of Muhammad (ﷺ) after the Dajjal (the Antichrist, al-Dajjal), in which Jesus, peace be upon him, will return. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) in the sound hadith made these two a single period from the afternoon until sunset.

Then Matthew said, in the rest of what passed of the Gospel in the copy from which I quoted, following what was mentioned earlier concerning the A'raf: "Jesus went up to Jerusalem and took the twelve. Then the mother of the two sons of Zebedee, namely James and John, came to him with her sons and bowed down before him. He said to her, 'What do you want?' She said, 'That one of my sons sit at your right hand and the other at your left in your kingdom.' Jesus answered, 'As for sitting at my right and my left, that is not mine to give, but it is for those for whom my Lord has prepared it.' When the ten heard this, they grew indignant with the other two (Mark said: 'with James and John'). Jesus called them and said, 'Do you not know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them? It shall not be so among you. Whoever wishes to be great among you shall be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave.'" Mark said: "He shall be last of all and servant of all. Even so, the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."

When he left Jericho, a great crowd followed him, and behold, two blind men were sitting by the road. They heard that Jesus was passing by, and they cried out, "Have mercy on us, O Lord, Son of David!" Jesus stopped, called them, and said, "What do you want me to do for you?" They said, "O Lord, that our eyes be opened." Jesus had compassion, touched their eyes, and at once they saw, and they followed him.

Mark's wording about this is: "He came to Jericho and left from there, and his disciples and a great crowd followed him. Behold, Bartimaeus son of Timaeus, the blind man, was sitting and asking about the road" (Luke said: "he was begging"). He heard the crowd passing by and asked, "What is this?" They told him that Jesus the Nazarene had come. Mark said: "When he heard that Jesus was approaching, he began to shout and say, 'O Jesus, Nazarene, son of David, have mercy on me!' They rebuked him so that he would be quiet, but he cried out all the more, 'O Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me!' Jesus stopped and said, 'Call him.' The blind man was called, and they said to him, 'Take heart and stand up, for he is calling you.' He threw off his cloak, rose, and came to Jesus. Jesus answered him and said, 'What do you want me to do for you?' The blind man said, 'O teacher' (Luke said: 'O Lord'), 'that I may see.' Jesus said to him, 'Go, your faith has saved you.' At once he saw, and followed him on the way" (Luke said: "glorifying God"). All the people who saw him gave praise to God.

He also said: "While he was journeying to Jerusalem, he passed between Samaria and Galilee. As he entered a certain village, ten lepers met him; they stood at a distance and raised their voices, saying, 'O Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!' He looked at them and said, 'Go and show yourselves to the priests.' As they were going, they were cleansed. When one of them saw that he had been cleansed, he returned with a loud voice glorifying God, and he fell on his face at his feet, giving thanks to him. He was a Samaritan. Jesus answered and said, 'Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Did none of them return to give glory to God except this foreigner?' Then he said to him, 'Rise and go; your faith has saved you.'"

Matthew said: When they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage at the Mount of Olives, and Mark said: at the gate of Bethphage and Bethany beside the Mount of Olives. Matthew said: Then Jesus sent two of his disciples, and said to them: "Go into the village that is before you, and you will find a donkey tied and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me. If anyone says anything to you, say: 'The Lord has need of them,' and he will send them at once." This was so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled, who said: "Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, humble, riding on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey." (p-320) The two disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them. They brought the donkey and the colt, laid their garments on them, and he sat upon them. A great crowd spread their garments on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. Mark's account of this is: "You will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. If anyone says to you, 'What are you doing with this?' say: 'The Lord has need of it,' and at once he will send it back here." They went and found the colt tied at the gate outside on the road, and they untied it. Some of those standing there said to them, "What are you doing?" They told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go. They brought the colt to Jesus, threw their garments upon it, and he sat upon it. Many spread their garments on the road, and others [cut] branches from the field and spread them on the road.

Matthew said: The crowds that went before him and those that followed cried out, saying: "Hosanna to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!" Mark said: "Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!" Luke said: When he drew near the descent of the Mount of Olives, the multitude of the notables and the disciples began [rejoicing and] praising God and glorifying him with every voice for all the mighty works they had seen, saying: "Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!" (p-321) Some of the Pharisees among the crowd said to him, "Teacher, rebuke your disciples." He said to them, "If these were silent, the stones would cry out." When he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it and said: "If you had known in this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes. Days will come upon you when your enemies will raise a bank around you, surround you, and press you on every side, and they will dash you to the ground and your children within you, and they will not leave in you one stone upon another."

Matthew said: When he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, saying, "Who is this?" The crowd said, "This is Jesus the prophet, from Nazareth of Galilee." Jesus entered the Temple of God and drove out all who sold and bought in the Temple, overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold doves, and said to them: "It is written: My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers." John said: Jesus went up to Jerusalem and found in the Temple those who sold oxen, sheep, and doves, and money-changers sitting. He made a whip of cords (p-322) and drove them all out of the Temple, driving out the oxen and the sheep, scattering the money-changers' coins, and overturning their tables. [And] Matthew said: Blind and lame people came to him in the Temple, and he healed them. The chief priests saw the wonders he performed and the children shouting in the Temple, "Hosanna to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!" They were indignant and said, "Do you not hear what these are saying?" Jesus said to them, "Yes. Have you never read: Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babes you have prepared praise?" He left them, went out of the city to Bethany, and spent the night there. The next day, as he returned to the city, he became hungry. He saw a fig tree by the road and went to it, but found nothing on it except leaves. He said to it: "May no fruit ever come from you again." Immediately the fig tree withered. When the disciples saw it, they marvelled and said, "How did the fig tree wither at once?" Jesus answered and said to them: "Truly I tell you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but if you say to this mountain, 'Be lifted up and cast into the sea,' it will be done." Mark said: "If you have faith in God, truly I tell you: whoever says to this mountain, 'Be moved and cast into this sea,' and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will happen, it will be his. Therefore I tell you: whatever you ask for in prayer with faith, you will receive it, and it will be yours." Matthew said: "Whatever you ask in prayer with faith, you will receive." Mark said: John said to him: "Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him because he did not follow us." Jesus said to them: "Do not forbid him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name can quickly speak evil of me. Whoever is not against you is for you. And whoever gives you a cup of water in the name of your Father, the Messiah, truly I tell you, his reward will not be lost."

In it, among what is not permissible to apply in our law (sharʿ, the revealed law), is the application of "Father" to God and "Lord" to others without restriction. The warning about the like of this has been given more than once before. And God is the guide to what is right.

Having established that the Messengers are callers to the Truth to their Lord, whether willingly or unwillingly, through the Book and the iron, and having established that all happiness lies in following them, and that innovations bring no good even if Satan adorns their matter and makes them appear to be good, and that the companions of the one who abrogated the law of those before him (Jesus) innovated an innovation thought to be good, so they were left to it and most of them became corrupt, this necessitated the sending of one who abrogates every law that preceded him with an abrogation that has no removal (p-324) for there is no prophet after him, and he forbade innovations with a prohibition no one before him had made similar to. This produced His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, meaning: affirm this with a sound affirmation, in a prophet from among those who came before, or in the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Fear Allah﴾, meaning: fear His punishment; so make between yourselves and His wrath—for He is the Supreme King—a shield by preserving courtesy toward Him, and do not feel secure from His scheme; so be on guard [against] His stripping you of what He has given you. So follow the Messenger and you will be safe, and hold fast to following him lest you perish. ﴿And believe in His Messenger﴾, meaning: the one for whom there is now no other messenger besides him, with a faith joined to your faith in Allah, for faith in Him is not valid except together with faith in His Messenger; and that you remain steadfast in faith in him, and join faith in him to faith in those who came before him, O People of the Book, because his message is universal; he has abrogated all the religions that preceded him. So beware lest a deviation from him, out of envy or otherwise, incline you away from him; so hasten to answer him and all cling to his caution, and do not incline at all toward any innovation. ﴿He will give you﴾ reward for following him, ﴿a double portion﴾, meaning: two great shares, ﴿of His mercy﴾, a protection for you from the punishment, just as the kifl (saddle-cloth) protects the rider from falling. The kifl is a cloth tied on the back of the camel, its front part placed on the withers and its rear part on the rump. This protection is for the sake of your faith in him (ﷺ) and your faith in those who came before him, along with lightness of works and the lifting of burdens; and it is [higher] in reward than one who did good in the Jahiliyyah. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to one who asked him about it: "You became Muslim with whatever good you had earlier."

It indicates that the two portions are by raising of ranks and the outpouring of special goods, by His saying: ﴿And He will make for you﴾, meaning: in addition to that, ﴿a light﴾, figurative in this world through success in works, from known matters and inner knowledge, and sensory in the Hereafter by means of works, ﴿by which you will walk﴾, meaning: figuratively in this world through success in works, and literally in the Hereafter by means of works.

Since man is not free of deficiency, and does not reach all that is due to the Merciful, He said: ﴿And He will forgive you﴾, meaning: [what] has passed from you of inadvertence and intention, of jest and earnestness. When He, exalted is He, established that, He followed it with the description that forgiveness and what follows it is an attribute of His encompassing all who He wills, so He said: ﴿And Allah﴾, meaning: the one encompassing all attributes of perfection, greatness, and majesty, ﴿is Forgiving﴾, meaning: exceedingly effacing of sin both in essence and in trace, ﴿Merciful﴾, meaning: exceedingly bountiful in honor toward whoever He forgives and enables to do works that please Him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 57, verse 29:

When the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) had followed their desires in hating the unlettered ones (al-ummiyyun, the Arabs), and their hearts had been steeped in the belief that prophethood was exclusive to them, because they are the descendants of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, through his cousin's daughter (ibnat ammihi), while the Arabs, although they too are his descendants, are from the Mother (al-Amah, Hajar), and they did not realize that their being descendants of his was a qualification for the prophethood of some of them, and that their being from the Mother was a preparation for the universality of the message, because of the universality of lineage, He said, indicating that they had become like cattle that perceive only sensible things, attaching the prepositional phrase to "they believed" (amanu) and "He will give you" (yu'tikum) and what follows it: ﴿So that the People of the Book may know﴾, meaning, so that they may know with great knowledge the content of His report, and its opposite is negated by what the added negative particle conveys. ﴿The People of the Book﴾, meaning, from the two groups who restricted themselves to their own book and their prophets and did not believe in the Final Prophet and what was revealed to him. ﴿That they﴾, meaning, that they are not ﴿able﴾, meaning at any time, ﴿to [obtain] anything﴾ [meaning even a little] ﴿of the bounty of Allah﴾, meaning of the Sovereign, the Most High, who has favored you with what He has favored you with, which is not withheld, nor is it [withheld] by giving to you [where] He removed prophethood from them and placed it among their cousins, Isma'il, peace be upon him, those whom they did not regard as worthy, so they would say: "They are the sons of the Mother (Amah), they are unlettered, and they have no claim over us." He made the prophethood with which He favored you universal, as indicated by what the word "son of the Mother" contains of inclusiveness through its relation and its branching out. And since they worked much and were given little, (ﷺ) said: "The Jews, from the beginning of the day, [were employed] for a qirat each, and the Christians from noon for a qirat each, and this Ummah from the afternoon prayer for two qirats each. The two groups said: 'Why do we do more work and receive less pay?' He said: 'Have I wronged you in any of your rights?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'That is My bounty, which I give to whom I will.'"

Ibn Burjan mentioned the meaning of this hadith, as was mentioned previously about him shortly before, from the Gospel, and applied it to it, and I mentioned it [myself] in al-A'raf. Imam [Ahmad] narrated it in several places in the Musnad, and al-Bukhari in seven places, in the chapters on prayer, hiring, the mention of the Children of Israel, the virtues of the Qur'an, and monotheism, and al-Tirmidhi in the chapter on parables, and he said: "Hasan sahih," from various routes, which I have combined in their wording, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Your example" (mathalukum). In this narration: "the example of this Ummah." In another narration: "the example of my Ummah." In another narration: "Your example and the example of the Jews and Christians is like a man." In another narration: "Your example and the example of the People of the Two Books is like a man who hired workers," and in another narration: "who hired laborers, and said: 'Who will work for me from the morning prayer [to ...]'" and in another narration: "from early morning until midday for a qirat. Then the Jews worked." In another narration: "The Jews said: 'We [will]'" and they worked. Then he said: "Who will work for me from midday until the afternoon prayer for a qirat?" Then the Christians did it. In another narration: "The Christians said: 'We [will]'" and they worked. Then he said: "Who will work for me from the afternoon prayer until sunset, for two qirats each? Indeed, you are the ones who worked." In another narration: "You work." In another narration: "And you, the Muslims, work from the afternoon prayer until night," and in another narration: "until the maghrib," and in another narration: "until sunset, for two qirats each. Surely you have a double reward." The Jews and Christians became angry and said: "We [...]" and in another narration: "What is with us? [We do] more work and receive less reward," and in another narration: "less pay." Allah the Exalted said: "Have I [...]" and in another narration: "And have I [...]" diminished [anything] of your right?" and in another narration: "of your reward at all?" They said: "No." He said: "Indeed it is [...]" and in another narration: "Indeed it is [only]" bounty. In another narration: "That is My bounty, which I give to whom I will." In another narration: "I give it to whom I wish."

In another narration: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was standing on the pulpit saying: "Indeed your remaining (baqa'akum) [is]" and in another narration: "Indeed your lifespan (baqa'akum)," and in another narration: "Indeed your term (ajalukum) is within the term of those who passed before you of the nations," and in another narration: "In what has preceded you of the nations, is like what is between the afternoon prayer and the maghrib," and in another narration: "until the sun sets." In another narration: "Indeed the likeness of your terms among the terms of the nations before you is like what is between the afternoon prayer and sunset," and in another narration: "until the setting," and in another narration: "until the sunsets." "The People of the Torah were given the Torah, and they acted upon it until midday, and then they were unable, so they were given a qirat [each]." "Then the People of the Gospel were given the Gospel, and they acted upon it until" (in another narration: "until") "the afternoon prayer," and in another narration: "until the afternoon prayer was performed. Then they were unable, so they were given a qirat each. Then you were given the Qur'an, and you acted upon it until the sun set," and in another narration: "[until the sun set]," "so you were given two qirats each." In another narration: "Then we were given the Qur'an, and we acted upon it until the sun set, so we were given two qirats each." The People of the Two Books said, in another narration: "the People of the Torah and the Gospel": "Our Lord, these people have done less work than us and received more reward," and in another narration: "compensation." In another narration: "O our Lord, You gave these two qirats each and gave us one qirat each, while we did more work than them." Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: "[Have I]" and in another narration: "Have I wronged you in any of your reward?" and in another narration: "of your wages?" They said: "No." He said: "It is My bounty, and in another narration: "That is My bounty, which I give to whom I will."

Some scholars took from this hadith what came before these nations and left their conditions in that state. He said: It indicates the people of Noah and Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, who had the night. The people of Noah were, at its beginning, in pure, long darkness, in which nothing of the first glimmers of light or signs of dawn had appeared to them, while Noah, peace be upon him, informed them of it and commanded them to prepare for it. For this reason his trial with them was prolonged, peace be upon him, and only a few believed with him. As for the people of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, they were as if they were at the end of the night, when the first glimmers of morning had appeared to them and the flashes of success had shone upon them. For this reason Lut, peace be upon him, believed, and likewise Sarah his wife, and his children by her and by others, all of them. Islam and prophethood continued among his descendants until Musa, peace be upon him, came, and his time was like the period between dawn and midday. His people were at times in one state and at times in another: at times they thought they were in light however they were, so they would turn aside to the right and left, becoming like those who enter caves, grottoes, and tunnels, and then come out of them and return to the light. Their mistakes were sometimes great and sometimes small. As for the people of Isa, peace be upon him, they were like one who is at midday in intense light, so error from him can only come from great blindness. For this reason their error was the most horrible and foul of errors. And Allah is the Granter of success.

﴿And that﴾, meaning, and so that you may know that ﴿the bounty﴾ [meaning] which one who possesses it does not need, ﴿is in the hand of Allah﴾, meaning He to whom all command belongs, ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾ from among them or from others [whether it is prophethood or something else].

And since perhaps someone might think that He only specifies it for those whom He wills because it cannot encompass all people, He repelled that by His saying: ﴿And Allah﴾, meaning He who encompasses all the attributes of perfection, ﴿is the Possessor of great bounty﴾, meaning its owner with an ownership that never separates from Him, and no one has any ownership of it alongside Him, nor any disposal of it in any way at all. Therefore He specifies whom He wills with what He wills, so no one can object in any way. All that is in the heavens and the earth has declared Him free of imperfection with the greatest declaration of transcendence, so He is the Mighty, the Wise, whom no one else is mighty and no one else is wise. Thus its end, as you see, corresponds to its beginning, and its detailed parts return to what joins them. And Allah is the Guide to what is right, and to Him is the return and the final place.
